Mecha equipment falls into several categories: flight systems, sensor systems, defense systems, weapons (both
hand-held and integrated), and miscellaneous systems.
Installing a piece of equipment on a mecha—be it a weapon or some other integrated system—requires a
Craft (mechanical) check (DC 20) and a Craft (electrical) check (DC 20). The check is made after investing an
amount of time determined by the mecha’s size: Large 10 minutes, Huge 30 minutes, Gargantuan 1 hour, Colossal
3 hours. If the weapon or system occupies more than one equipment slot on the mecha, multiply the installation
time by the number of slots it takes up. An integrated weapon or system can be removed in half the time with a
successful Repair check (DC 20).
In addition to a general description, each piece of equipment includes the following information:
Equipment Slots: The number of equipment slots needed to install the equipment. Some pieces of equipment are
limited to specific body slots, as noted here.
Activation: How long it takes to activate the piece of equipment (usually a standard action).
Range/Range Increment: A range listing indicates the maximum distance out to which the equipment functions. If
a range increment is listed instead, it represents the distance at which accuracy begins to decline, as per the rules
on range increments. Unless otherwise noted, equipment with a range increment has a maximum of ten
increments.
Target or Targets/Effect/Area: This entry starts with one of three headings: Target, Effect, or Area. If the target of
the component is You, you do not receive a saving throw (and there is no saving throw entry for the piece of
equipment). If a component is a weapon capable of autofire, it will be noted here.
Duration: The amount of time a piece of equipment continues to operate before it needs to be reactivated, or how
long its effect lasts. A duration of persistent means the equipment functions until the mecha is destroyed (reduced
to 0 hit points) or the mecha’s operator turns it off (usually as a free action).
Saving Throw: If a piece of equipment calls for a saving throw, the type of saving throw is listed here, along with
the effect of a successful save.
Purchase DC: The purchase DC for the Wealth check to acquire the equipment.
Restriction: The level of license required to purchase the equipment legally.
Leave Room for the Pilot
When equipping a mecha from scratch, make sure to leave vacant equipment slots for the mecha operator’s
cockpit. (The cost of the cockpit is already factored into the mecha’s base purchase DC.) For a Medium mecha, the
operator always occupies the torso. On Large mecha and Huge mecha, the operator always occupies two
equipment slots: the torso, and any one other adjoining equipment slot (this assumes the pilot is Medium; if the
intended pilot is Small, then the Pilot’s Cockpit is only one slot).
On Gargantuan and Colossal mecha, the designer has more choice when placing the operator’s cockpit.
However, the two slots must be adjoining slots (not the left arm and the right leg, for example). Copilot and
passenger cockpits are described under Miscellaneous Equipment.
In the case of a power armor, the pilot is the same size category as the power armor, meaning it occupies
for more of the interior than a smaller pilot in a mecha. This means less slots are available to power armors
because of the space that will be occupied by the pilot’s body. Each mecha is noted with the slot requirements for 587
mecha versus power armor pilots.

Sensor systems make it easier for mecha operators to perceive their surroundings; however, not all mecha are
equipped with sensors (or even require them). In such cases, mecha operators must rely on their own acute vision
and hearing.
A mecha equipped with sensors conducts passive scans of the surrounding area constantly, without the
operator’s attention. A passive scan extends in all directions at once, providing the operator with data on
surrounding terrain, obstacles, and the location of other creatures, vehicles, and mecha within several miles of the
mecha’s position.
A sensor system can also be used to conduct an active scan of a single target. With a successful Computer
Use check (DC 15) and a move action, a mecha’s operator can use the onboard sensor system to actively scan a
single nonliving target (usually another mecha or vehicle) and determine specific information about that target, as
specified in the sensor system’s description.
To build a sensor system from scratch, a character must succeed at a Craft (electrical) check (DC 30) after
investing 60 hours in its assembly. A character without an electrical tool kit takes a –4 penalty on the skill check.

The R-XI “Archie” Anti-Missile Targeting System is a specialized sensor system dedicated to detecting and
attacking incoming missiles. Once per round, the defense system can attempt to shoot down an incoming missile,
using an integrated weapon system with autofire capability (typically a Pop-Up Autolaser; see below).
As soon as a missile targeting the mecha gets within the Archie’s closest range increment (dependent on
the autofire weapon assigned to the Archie), the R-XI attacks the missile with the autofire weapon assigned to it.
The R-XI shoots down one incoming missile per round by burst-firing the 10’ radius (2-polyhex) area that the
missile is in, forcing the missile to make a Reflex save DC (15 + the Sensor System Class) in order to avoid being hit
(a Class I System makes it a DC 16 Reflex save, while a Class V System makes it a DC 20 Reflex save for the missile).
If the missile is hit, then it is destroyed or otherwise caused to deviate, and the mecha is not hit. Missiles
with blast areas are sufficiently destroyed to prevent them from exploding properly, and they do not explode to
any effect; they simply crash from the sky.
While the Archie Anti-Missile Targeting System is engaged, the weapon system it is controlling cannot be
used by the pilot or co-pilot for attacking; the R-XI must be disengaged (a move action) to use the weapon to
attack anything other than a missile. Also note that the Archie can determine which missiles will hit its mecha, and
thus it only attacks those missiles that are going to hit, prioritizing direct hits as “primary” targets and splash hits as
“secondary” targets.

Size: The size of the weapon being wielded. In the case of a melee weapon, the weapon is always scaled to the

much larger and stronger than they would otherwise be, and they can wield truly frightening weapons. However,
they still obey the essential rules of movement and combat. They still threaten hexes within their reach, take move
actions and attack actions, duck behind cover to gain a bonus to Defense, and so forth. In some respects, however,
mecha movement and combat differs from character movement and combat. The following sections describe
specific situations that arise when mecha maneuver and clash on the battlefield.

It takes a full-round action to climb into a mecha’s cockpit and a move action to activate its various systems so it
can move and fight. It takes a full-round action to get out of a mecha unless an HV-5 Haven escape pod or similarly
expeditious device is used (see Miscellaneous Equipment).

Mecha operators use the Drive skill to operate their mecha on the ground and the Pilot skill to operate their mecha
in the air or in space.
In general, mecha operators don’t need to make Drive or Pilot checks to steer their mecha around the
battlefield. However, these skills may come into play in combat under the following circumstances:
• When trying to move past a foe without provoking an attack of opportunity, a mecha operator can make a Drive
check or Pilot check (as appropriate) instead of a Tumble check.
• A mecha operator can oppose a trip attempt with a Drive check (if on the ground) or a Pilot check (if in the air).
• A successful Pilot check can pull a mecha out of a stall (see Flying Mecha, below).
• A character in a copilot cockpit can use the aid another action, making Drive or Pilot checks (as appropriate) to
aid the Drive and Pilot checks of the mecha’s operator.

The vehicle rules are entirely appropriate for ground cars and other normal modes of transportation; however,
even a clumsy mecha is more maneuverable than a normal vehicle.
On the ground, mecha move as characters. They can turn at any time, move in any direction, and stop on
a dime. In the air, though, they are more limited.
Most flying mecha have to slow down to make a turn, and many are limited to fairly wide turns and must
maintain a minimum forward speed. Each flying mecha has a maneuverability rating, as shown on Table: Flight
Maneuverability. A mecha’s flight systems determine its maneuverability.
Minimum Forward Speed: If a flying mecha fails to maintain its minimum forward speed, it must land at the end of
its movement. If it is too high above the ground to land, it falls straight down, descending 150 feet in the first
round of falling. If this distance brings it to the ground, it takes falling damage. If the fall doesn’t bring the mecha
to the ground, the operator must succeed at a Pilot check (DC 20) to recover. Otherwise, it falls another 300 feet. If
it hits the ground, it takes falling damage. Otherwise, it has another chance to recover on its next turn.
Hover: The ability to stay in one place while airborne.
Fly Backward: The ability to fly backward.
Reverse: A mecha with good maneuverability uses up 5 feet of its speed to start flying backward.
Turn: How much the flying mecha can turn after covering the stated distance.
Turn in Place: A mecha with good or average maneuverability can “spend” some of its speed to turn in place.
Maximum Turn: How much the mecha can turn in any one space.
Up Angle: The angle at which the mecha can ascend.
Up Speed: How fast the mecha can ascend.
Down Angle: The angle at which the mecha can descend.
Down Speed: A flying mecha can descend at twice its normal flying speed.
Between Down and Up: An average, poor, or clumsy mecha must fly level for a minimum distance after
descending and before ascending. Any flying mecha can begin descending after an ascent without an intervening
distance.

Only a mecha equipped with space skin (see Miscellaneous Equipment) can operate in outer space. However, the
mecha’s operator takes a –4 penalty on all attack rolls and skill checks unless she has the Zero-G Training feat or
has equipped her mecha with a zero-g stabilizer.
In outer space, mecha fly just like they do in the atmosphere, with three exceptions. First, all flying mecha
improve by one maneuverability category (clumsy becomes poor, poor becomes average, average becomes good,
and so on). Second, all mecha can ascend and descend regardless of the limitations on Table: Flight
Maneuverability, and their speed is unchanged if they do so. Finally, all mecha can hover in space and need not
maintain a minimum forward speed.

As Tech constructs, mecha and power armor are susceptible to critical hits. To confirm a critical against a mecha,
the mecha’s full Armor Class, for purposes of confirming a critical, is equal to their touch Armor class plus one-half
the mecha’s Hardness (rounded up), plus the pilot’s Defense Bonus plus their Shield equipment AC modifier,
assuming the pilot is proficient in both the mecha and in the shield. Other modifiers might include the pilot’s luck
or insight bonuses to Armor Class.
Whenever you confirm a critical hit against a mecha, you may choose to roll a d20 and consult Table:
Mecha Critical Hits instead of dealing the normal critical hit damage for the attack. However, you must accept the
results of the roll, even if those results are less than desirable.
Table: Mecha Critical Hits
d20 Roll Effect(s)
1–3 Normal damage, crew dazed
4–7 Normal damage, equipment damaged
8–9 Normal critical hit, crew dazed
10 Normal damage, equipment destroyed
11-12 Normal critical hit, mecha knocked prone
13 Crew hit (normal damage)
14-16 Normal critical hit, slot damaged
17-18 Normal critical hit, slot destroyed
19 Severe critical hit, mecha knocked prone
20 Severe critical hit, mecha stunned
Normal Damage: The attack deals normal damage (do not apply critical hit multipliers).
Crew Dazed: Each crewmember aboard the mecha, including its operator, must succeed on a Fortitude save (DC
15) or be dazed for 1 round. Unable to act, a dazed character can take no actions, but still retains their full Defense
Bonus.
Equipment Damaged: One piece of equipment (attacker’s choice) is damaged and ceases to function until
repaired. It can be a flight system, sensor system, defense system, weapon (handheld or integrated), or 617
miscellaneous system. Repairing a damaged system requires 1 hour of work and a successful Repair check (DC 20).
Normal Critical Hit: Roll critical hit damage normally.
Equipment Destroyed: One piece of equipment (attacker’s choice) is destroyed and ceases to function. It can be a
flight system, sensor system, defense system, weapon (handheld or integrated), or miscellaneous system. A
destroyed system cannot be repaired, only replaced.
Mecha Knocked Prone: The force of the attack knocks the mecha prone. All crewmembers and passengers aboard
take 1d6 points of bludgeoning damage as they are knocked about their cockpits. A prone mecha takes a –4
penalty on melee attack rolls and can’t use thrown ranged weapons. The mecha gains a +4 bonus to Defense
against ranged attacks, but takes a –4 penalty to Defense against melee attacks. Standing up from prone is a move
action that provokes attacks of opportunity.
Crew Hit: The attack bypasses the mecha’s structure. Apply normal damage to one crewmember or passenger
(determined randomly), ignoring the mecha’s hit points; only apply the mecha’s hardness.
Slot Damaged: One of the mecha’s equipment slots (attacker’s choice) is damaged. Any piece of equipment wholly
or partially installed in that slot will not function until the slot is repaired. Repairing a damaged equipment slot
requires 1 hour of work and a successful Repair check (DC 25).
Slot Destroyed: One of the mecha’s equipment slots (attacker’s choice) is destroyed, along with any piece of
equipment wholly or partially installed in it. Rebuilding a destroyed equipment slot requires 12 hours of work and
a successful Craft (mechanical) check (DC 30).
Severe Critical Hit: Roll critical hit damage using a x5 multiplier instead of the weapon’s normal multiplier.
Mecha Stunned: The mecha automatically drops what it is holding and can take no attack or move actions for 1
round. While the mecha is stunned, the operator is not stunned).

library.t: RANGED ATTACKS AND ATTACKS OF OPPORTUNITY
library.d:
Mecha only provoke attacks of opportunity from creatures of their own size or larger (including other mecha)
when they fire a ranged weapon in a threatened area.

Any piece of mecha equipment integrated into a mecha’s hand slot—and only the hand slot—can be stowed
magnetically against the mecha or in a storage compartment as a move action. This frees up the hand to perform
more delicate manipulation (such as opening a door or pressing a button) or grabbing another piece of mecha
equipment. A mecha may have more pieces of equipment for its hand slots than it has hand slots available; it just
can’t use them all at once.
Essential Mecha Feats
A character without the Mecha Operation feat and Mecha Weapon Proficiency feat suffers serious penalties while
operating a mecha of any size. The penalties for not having these feats are summarized below:
Mecha Operation: A character without this feat takes a –4 penalty on Balance, Climb, Drive, Escape Artist, Hide,
Move Silently, Pilot, and Tumble checks when operating a mecha. Furthermore, they do not apply their Defense
Bonus to the full AC of the mecha, nor can they run or charge.
Mecha Weapon Proficiency: A character without this feat takes a –4 penalty on attack rolls made while operating
a mecha. Furthermore, the character cannot apply the various firearm feats (such as Advanced Firearms
Proficiency, Dead Aim, Double Tap, Shot on the Run, and Strafe) to a mecha’s ranged weapons.
Mecha and Feats
If you have the Mecha Weapon Proficiency feat, any feats that apply to firearms (such as Double Tap and Strafe)
also apply to relevant ranged mecha weapons.
Melee-oriented feats from the Brawl and Combat Martial Arts trees don’t apply if you’re operating a
mecha; they do in a power armor if proficient (i.e. Power Armor Proficiency). A character with the Mecha
Operation feat threatens all areas within reach of the mecha, and making a slam attack with a mecha doesn’t
provoke an attack of opportunity.
Feats from the Defense Martial Arts tree function normally for characters in mecha.

Size / TS / Type: The mecha’s body size, its Tech Scale, and its type (mecha and/or power armor).
Hit Points / Dice: The hit points of the mecha, also presented in Dice (“d”), units of 5 hit points.
Superstructure: The chief material used in the construction of the mecha’s superstructure, along with its Hardness
in pips and dice.
Armor: The type of armor installed on the mecha, with its modifier to Armor Class and its armor penalty modifier
(if any); apply this penalty to the operator’s Balance, Climb, Escape Artist, Hide, Jump, Move Silently, and Tumble
checks. Some types of armor also reduce a mecha’s speed. 619
Touch/Full AC (T/AC): The mecha’s touch Armor Class, the attack result required to hit it, and its full Armor Class,
the confirmation result required to score a critical hit against it.
Note that the Touch Armor Class scores given for power armor templates only include the power armor’s
size penalty. The pilot must still incorporate any Dexterity modifiers (as per the power armor’s maximum Dex
allowable), dodge modifier(s), and/or deflection AC modifiers, amongst possible others.
The full Armor Class of a mecha, for the purpose of confirming a critical, is equal to their Touch AC plus
one-half of the mecha’s Hardness (rounded up), plus the Defense Bonus of the proficient pilot, plus possibly a
shield modifier. In the case of the examples given here, the full AC is the Touch AC plus ½ the mecha’s Hardness
plus any Shield equipment AC bonuses.
Strength (Min): The Strength attribute of the mecha or power armor. As a power armor, the pilot uses the
mecha’s Strength or the pilot’s Strength, whichever is higher. Thus, this score represents the minimum Strength
attribute of the power armor pilot while in the power armor
Dexterity (Max): The Dexterity attribute of the mecha or power armor. The pilot uses the mecha’s Dexterity or the
pilot’s Dexterity, whichever is lower. Thus, this score represents the maximum Dexterity attribute of the mecha
pilot while piloting the mecha or power armor.
Speed: The mecha’s base land speed (and fly speed, if applicable). As a power armor, the mecha’s land speed is
equal to the wearer’s land speed, minus any speed modifiers for the power armor.
Space / Reach: The mecha’s occupied space and its threatened area within its reach.
Slam: The mecha’s inherent Slam attack, with any modifiers from size noted.
Equipment Slots: The slots available to the mecha for integrated weapons, sensors, and other systems. Any slot
marked with an asterisk (“*”) is not available to a power armor of that size, as those slots are instead part of the

Chapter IV: Starships
Built to traverse the sidereal spaces between the stars, starships serve a multitude of purposes in both the near
and the far-flung future. Where starfaring races encounter one another, the state of nature takes hold, and the
races will quickly appraise one another’s capabilities to determine the magnitude of the threat. In many cases, war
breaks out, as the competition for resources continues at a galactic level.
634

Starships are vehicles built to withstand the desolate vacuum of space while offering travelers relative safety over
the requisite time it takes to travel from one celestial body to another. All starships are considered Tech
Constructs.
There are five main sizes of starship; ultralight, light, mediumweight, heavy, and superheavy. Amongst
each of those five sizes there are a range of starship subtypes based on a ship’s purpose. These types and their
respective subtypes are;

Unless otherwise noted, a starship always divides its capital dice (“D”) evenly amongst the five sections of
the ship; infrastructure (IS), fore, starboard, port, and aft.
Each of the starship subtypes has its own predefined characteristics for the typical length, weight, crew,
passenger capacity, and cargo capacity, as well as how many capital dice the ship subtype has. Templates are
available at the end of this chapter to help you design your own starships, based on one of the subtypes given
above and the Tech Scale of the scenario.
The other aspects of a starship that are more dependent on the Tech Scale available include the ship’s
engines, weapons, armor, defense systems, sensor systems, and communications systems. All starships have one 635
type of armor, up to two communication systems, and up to two grappling systems (but each grappling system
counts as a weapons selection). A ship’s size determines how many slots it has for each of the other types of tech
(i.e. engines, weapons, defense systems, and sensor systems).

A starship’s engine determines how fast the ship moves. The more efficient the engine, the faster it can move the
ship—and the more expensive it is. In addition, certain low-tech engines burn fuel of some sort, limiting the range
and increasing the operational cost. In space, fuel-burning engines rely on vector jets to adjust their course, using
fuel only in short, controlled burns to increase momentum.
To build a starship engine from scratch, a character must succeed at a Craft (electrical) check, a Craft
(mechanical) check, and a Craft (structural) check, all (DC 30), after investing 120 hours in its assembly. A character
without an appropriate tool kit takes a –4 penalty on that skill check. The character must also spend Wealth equal
to the engine’s base purchase DC.
Installing an engine requires a successful Craft (mechanical) check (DC 30) after investing 60 hours in the
process. A character without a mechanical tool kit takes a –4 penalty on the skill check.
The various types of engines are listed below.
Minimum Ship Size: The minimum size the starship must be to have this type of engine.
Tactical Speed Bonus: The bonus that the engine provides to the starship’s tactical speed, given in feet and hexes.
Unless otherwise noted, a starship’s base movement rate is 3,000 feet / move action; with two move actions per
round, that’s 6,000 feet / round.
Purchase DC: The engine’s purchase DC.

THRUSTERS (TS 5)
Thrusters can propel a ship through a planetary atmosphere and land it safely on a planetary surface. Thrusters
also serve as secondary engines when primary engines fail or shut down. Common types of thrusters include the
scramjet, chemical rocket, repulsion thrust, or powered airfoil, although the exact form doesn’t matter.
A ship with thrusters as its primary source of propulsion must refuel after every battle or every orbital
mission. Thruster fuel has a purchase DC of 31.
Minimum Ship Size: Huge.
Tactical Speed Bonus: +0 feet.
Purchase DC: 10 + one-half the base purchase DC of the starship.
FUSION TORCH (TS 6)
This engine consists of a fusion reactor with one wall of the magnetic bottle missing, directing the thrust in the
form of super-heated plasma. The fusion torch is intended for space-only applications; its exhaust stream would
melt anything it landed on and incinerate everything within a few hundred yards of ground zero; it also expels a
tremendous amount of radiation. Many ships fitted with fusion torch rockets use thrusters for atmospheric travel.
Otherwise, they must remain permanently in space, relying on shuttlecraft to reach a planet’s surface. The fusion
torch uses hydrogen for fuel. 636
A ship using a fusion torch as its primary source of propulsion must refuel after every three battles or
interplanetary trips. Fusion torch fuel has a purchase DC of 23.
Minimum Ship Size: Gargantuan.
Tactical Speed Bonus: +500 feet (+2 hexes).
Purchase DC: 10 + one-half the base purchase DC of the starship.
ION ENGINE (TS 6)
The ion engine generates power to break down molecules of a fuel material to create ions, and then expels them
by means of a magnetic impeller. It doesn’t provide as effective a mass-thrust ratio as the fusion torch, but it’s
more fuel efficient, and its exhaust is not nearly as dangerous. Ion engines don’t function in any kind of
atmosphere, so most ships with this kind of power plant also come equipped with thrusters.
A ship using an ion engine as its primary source of propulsion must refuel after every five battles or
interplanetary trips. Ion engine fuel has a purchase DC of 29.
Minimum Ship Size: Huge.
Tactical Speed Bonus: +500 feet (+2 hexes).
Purchase DC: 15 + one-half the base purchase DC of the starship.
PHOTON SAILS (TS 6)
Photon sails are immense but extremely fragile foil structures only a few molecules thick. Light pressure from a
nearby star (or laser drive station, when available) provides motive force. The sails’ acceleration rates drop to half
if the ship is beyond the edge of a star system and drop to one-quarter if the only available light is starlight. The
sails can be wrecked by minor damage, but every ship equipped with photon sails carries at least three spare sets.
Unfortunately, it takes 12 hours to replace damaged sails, though deployment or stowage of the sails takes only 1
minute.
In combat, any weapon hit against a sail-driven starship destroys the deployed photon sails and prevents
the ship from moving until the sails are replaced. The sail-ship continues on its last course and retains its former
speed until the sails are replaced. Accordingly, most sail-ships carry a secondary propulsion system (such as
thrusters or an ion engine) for emergency maneuvering and sailing against the sun. Photon sails are completely
useless in atmosphere—in fact, they’re instantly destroyed by atmospheric entry—making a secondary propulsion
system a virtual necessity for most sail-ships.
Minimum Ship Size: Gargantuan.
Tactical Speed Bonus: None.
Purchase DC: 10 + one-quarter the base purchase DC of the starship (per set of photon sails).
INDUCTION ENGINE (TS 7)
Hands-down the best engine available at this or any previous Tech Scale, the induction engine uses artificial gravity
to provide incredible thrust and maneuverability. The induction engine requires no fuel and produces no exhaust,
ideal for atmospheric, orbital, or deep-space work.
Minimum Ship Size: Huge.
Tactical Speed Bonus: +1,000 feet (+4 hexes).
Purchase DC: 15 + one-half the base purchase DC of the starship.
PARTICLE IMPULSE ENGINE (TS 7)
The particle impulse engine is the next evolutionary step of the TS 6 ion engine. It uses magnetic fields to produce
a constant stream of high-energy particles, as well as to provide vectored thrust. The major advancement of the
particle impulse drive over the ion drive is that the particle impulse engine uses a negligible amount of fuel, which
it also manufactures. The drive’s reaction is so efficient that the tiny amounts of matter present in interplanetary
or interstellar space can be collected through weak magnetic fields and converted into a thrust medium. Better
still, the particle impulse engine is capable of atmospheric entry. It causes some damage to any surface close to its
exhaust ports, but nowhere near as much damage as TS 6 engines do.
Minimum Ship Size: Gargantuan.
Tactical Speed Bonus: +1,000 feet (+4 hexes).
Purchase DC: 10 + one-half the base purchase DC of the starship. 637
GRAVITIC REDIRECTOR (TS 8)
A refinement of the induction engine, the gravitic redirector creates a gravitic singularity—essentially, a sub-
microscopic black hole—in the vicinity of the ship, producing a constant pull on the ship. By changing the location
of the singularity relative to the ship, the pilot can change the direction of the ship’s travel. The gravitic redirector
is more powerful and more efficient than the induction engine, and at the height of the technology’s heyday,
virtually foolproof. A gravitic redirector does not operate within a planetary atmosphere, and most ships fitted
with this kind of engine also have secondary thrusters or rely on shuttlecraft.
Minimum Ship Size: Colossal.
Tactical Speed Bonus: +1,500 feet (+6 hexes).
Purchase DC: 10 + one-half the base purchase DC of the starship.
INERTIAL FLUX ENGINE (TS 8)
By precisely controlling the quantum energy level of every atom on the ship simultaneously, the inertial flux engine
assumes the inertial states necessary to produce motion in any direction. In effect, by operating the controls, the
pilot chooses from instant to instant what vector the ship’s atoms will next possess, and the inertial flux engine
alters them simultaneously—along with everything else aboard, including the crew and passengers. An inertial flux
engine does not operate within a planetary atmosphere, and most ships fitted with this kind of engine also have
secondary thrusters or rely on shuttlecraft.
Minimum Ship Size: Gargantuan.
Tactical Speed Bonus: +1,500 feet (+6 hexes).
Purchase DC: 15 + one-half the base purchase DC of the starship.

Interlocking plates of light vanadium alloy absorb a respectable amount of damage and are easy to mold to a
starship’s hull.
Hardness: 30.
AC Modifier: +6.
Tactical Speed Penalty: None.
Weight: One-eighth the weight of the starship (rounded down).
Purchase DC: 15 + one-half the base purchase DC of the starship.
Restriction: Military (+3).
CERAMETAL (TS 7)
Combining the heat-resistant qualities of tough ceramics with the ductile strength of metal, cerametal armor offers
a good compromise between protection and economy.
Hardness: 30.
AC Modifier: +6.
Tactical Speed Penalty: None.
Weight: One-eighth the weight of the starship (rounded down).
Purchase DC: 10 + one-half the base purchase DC of the starship.
Restriction: Licensed (+1).

Starship weapons fall into one of four categories: beam weapons, projectile weapons, missiles, and mines. Each
category of weapon is described in greater detail below.
Starship weapons require the Starship Gunnery feat to operate proficiently. Without this feat, a gunner
takes a –4 penalty on attack rolls made with starship weapons. Trained, expert, and ace crew gunners are assumed
to have this feat.
To build a starship weapon system from scratch, a character must succeed at a Craft (electrical) check (DC
30) and a Craft (mechanical) check (DC 30) after investing 300 hours in its assembly. A character without the
appropriate tool kit takes a –4 penalty on that skill check. The character must also spend Wealth equal to the
weapon’s base purchase DC. 640
Installing a weapon system requires a successful Craft (electrical) check (DC 30) and a Craft (mechanical)
check (DC 30) after investing 30 hours. A character without the appropriate tool kit takes a –4 penalty on that skill
check.
Improving Older Tech Weapons: Certain beam and projectile weapons—as noted in Table: Starship Weapons—
can be upgraded for different rates of fire. These weapons can be reconfigured for semiautomatic or automatic
fire mode if developed by a higher Tech Scale society than the minimum Tech Scale required for that weapon.
Weapons can be purchased in their modified versions, but the purchase DC of a modified weapon increases by +3.

Beam weapons deal energy damage, usually of a nonspecific type. They range from weapons as simple as a high-
powered laser to monstrous devices capable of harnessing the fundamental forces of the universe.
Beam weapons draw power from a starship’s power plant and are considered to have unlimited
ammunition. However, many use capacitor technologies that need to recharge after each shot, limiting the rate of
fire to once per round (“Single” shots only).
Beam Weapon Mounts: Beam weapons are mounted on turrets or in banks that allow the weapons to fire in any
direction. The cost of a turret mount or bank is included in the purchase DC of the weapon. If desired, a weapon
can be set into a cupola offering any two adjacent firing arcs (Fore/Starboard, Fore/Port, Aft/Starboard, or
Aft/Port), reducing the Purchase DC by -1, or mounted in a fixed turret with a single firing arc (Fore, Starboard,
Port, or Aft), reducing the Purchase DC of the weapon by -2. (Missile launchers can fire in any direction; see Missile
Launchers.)

Projectiles are generally solid slugs delivered to the target, where the velocity and density of the slug hopefully
punch through the target’s defenses. The most basic projectile weapons launch a small hunk of metal at roughly
the speed of sound; the most advanced can push around mountains or molecules at greater than the speed of
light.
Starships have sufficient storage space to contain a virtually unlimited supply of projectile weapon
ammunition.
Projectile Weapon Mounts: Like beam weapons, projectile weapons are mounted on turrets or in banks that allow
the weapons to fire in any direction. The cost of a turret mount or bank is included in the purchase DC of the
weapon. If desired, a weapon can be set into a cupola offering any two adjacent firing arcs (Fore/Starboard,
Fore/Port, Aft/Starboard, or Aft/Port), reducing the Purchase DC by -1, or mounted in a fixed turret with a single
firing arc (Fore, Starboard, Port, or Aft), reducing the Purchase DC of the weapon by -2. (Missile launchers can fire
in any direction; see Missile Launchers.)

If a starship weapon has an automatic rate of fire, it can be set on autofire. Autofire affects an area and everything
in it, not a specific target. The starship using the autofire weapon targets a 1,000-foot-by-1,000-foot-by-1,000-foot
cubic area and makes an attack roll; the targeted area has an effective Armor Class of 10. If the attack succeeds,
the pilots of all ships within the affected area must make a Pilot check (DC 15) or take the weapon’s damage.
Apply a penalty on the Pilot skill check based on the size of the pilot’s ship: Gargantuan -0, Colossal
(Ultralight) –4, Colossal (Light) –8, Colossal (Medium) –12, Colossal (Heavy) –16, and Colossal (Superheavy) –20.
Autofire can also be used to shoot down missiles. To successfully hit an incoming (battery barrage of)
missile(s) with an autofire weapon is an effective Armor Class of 20. If the attack succeeds, each of the missiles in
the affected area must make an automated Pilot check (DC 15) or take the weapon’s damage. Non-AI missiles
have a modifier to their Pilot check equal to the Class of the sensor system on-board the ship firing the missiles. AI
missiles have their Pilot skill modifier plus the Class of the sensor system on-board the ship firing the missiles.

A starship missile is an explosive warhead fixed to a guided rocket and fired from a missile launcher. The type of
warhead determines both the type and amount of damage. Unless otherwise noted, a missile has a tactical speed
of 5,000 feet (20 hexes) per move action, 10,000 feet (40 hexes) per round, and it explodes with a radius of 5’ per 2
dice of damage. For example, a missile that does 16d6 damage has an explosion radius of 16 dice / 2 = 8 x 5’ = 40’ 641
blast radius.
A typical starship missile has the same hardness as the ship launching it, and 20 hp / 4d / 1D. All missiles
are equipped with guidance systems that, in conjunction with the ship’s sensor system, negate the penalty for
range increments. Depending on the range between the ship firing the missile and its target, the missile(s) may be
in transit for a full round or longer, giving the defending ship an opportunity to shoot down the missile(s). Missiles
are purchased in racks of eight.
Missile Launchers: A starship must be equipped with missile launchers to fire missiles. Each type of missile has its
own type of missile launcher; for example, a launcher designed to fire CHE missiles cannot fire KE submunition
missiles. In the vastness of space a missile launches in any direction, and its self-propulsion and internal guidance
ensure that it can effectively go in any direction. A missile launcher is therefore always omnidirectional: it cannot
be set into a cupola or a fixed turret, and it receives no purchase DC reduction for one. A missile launcher has a
purchase DC of 20.
Artificially-Intelligent Missiles (TS 7): Artificially intelligent (AIM) missiles are available as of Tech Scale 7. They are
effectively robots with an independent Class I Sensor system and a skill net for the skills Knowledge (technology),
Navigate, and Pilot. A dodged AIM missile will correct course for another attack (maneuverability poor), and thus
must be either shot down or outmaneuvered to cause it to crash into something else. This upgrade can be
purchased for an additional +3 to the missile’s base Purchase DC.

Mines are immobile explosives that must be deployed to be effective. Mines are equipped with sensors to scan
approaching ships and detonate when hostile ships draw near. Some mines also come equipped with cloaking
screens and other defensive systems to conceal their presence (see Defensive Systems).
Mines are sold individually. Although a mine weighs no more than a few thousand pounds, one mine
consumes 100 tons of a ship’s cargo capacity (most of it taken up by the launch system and radiation shielding).
Minelayers: A starship must be equipped with a minelayer (purchase DC 25) to deploy mines, and only Colossal
ships can be fitted with minelayers. A minelayer consists of two or more mine rails—low-powered magnetic
accelerators that can deploy one mine per round.
Deploying a Mine: A starship equipped with a minelayer can, as an attack action, deploy a single mine in any 250-
foot hex it occupies. Only after the starship leaves the mine’s detonation area does the mine activate.
A starship that deploys a mine sets the conditions under which the mine detonates. One mine can be
deployed per 250-foot hex, but it can be programmed to detonate simultaneously with any other mines that are
within its detonation area, if desired.
A deployed mine is a Medium-size object with Armor Class 5, hardness 20, and 40 hit points. Damaging or
destroying a deployed mine has a 50% chance per hit of detonating it.
Detonating a Mine: When certain predetermined conditions are met (usually when an enemy ship enters the
mine’s detonation area), the deployed mine explodes. The mine’s detonation area is typically a 4-polyhex (the hex
it occupies and the surrounding 3 rows of adjacent 250-foot hexes (37 250-foot hexes in total). All ships within the
mine’s detonation area take damage when the mine detonates. A pilot may attempt a Pilot check (DC 25) to
reduce the damage by half; making this check does not count as an action.

Fire-linked weapons are identical beam weapons or projectile weapons that point and fire in the same direction. In
effect, this arrangement creates a single weapon (fired with a single attack roll) that deals greater damage than
any one of its weapons alone. A fire link of eight or more weapons is the starship’s main cannon (see below).
Each full doubling of the number of fire-linked weapons (two weapons, four, eight, and so on) adds one
more multiple of the weapon’s base damage and increases the weapon’s size one size category. A twin-linked
weapon deals ×2 its base damage, a quad-linked weapon ×3, and an octo-linked weapon (a main cannon) ×4.
Multiply the capital dice the same way, so a [1d3D] weapon deals [2d3D] twin-linked and [3d3D] quad-linked. For
example, a Gargantuan-size fighter using twin-linked lasers (normally a Huge weapon inflicting 8d8 damage) deals
16d8 points of damage with a successful attack, and it is considered a Gargantuan weapon. Each doubling adds +3
to the purchase DC of the weapon; taking the above example, each twin-linked laser would have a purchase DC of
32 instead of 29.
Because the damage of a fire link is dealt as one hit, a target’s hardness is subtracted from it once, not 642
once per weapon. Against heavily armored targets, concentrated fire is the armor-cracker.
Variable fire links are also available in fire links of four or more weapons, allowing the gunner to decide
from attack to attack whether to fire the weapons individually (as normal), in a full link (as described above), or in
a partial link. A partial link allows the pilot to fire the linked weapons in groups of two. Only quad-linked weapons
or larger can be fired in a partial link.
Owing to power demands, a starship can only have one weapon effectively multiplied to octo-linked (8
fire-linked weapons) or higher, referred to as the starship’s “main cannon”. At full power an octo-linked main
cannon deals ×4 its base damage. If desired, it can instead fire at 25% power (2 weapons, equivalent to twin-
linked: ×2 base damage) or at 50% power (4 weapons, equivalent to quad-linked: ×3 base damage). The main
cannon also has a greater chance of scoring a critical hit (+1 to the threat range of the standard version weapon).
The main cannon always has a single rate of fire, regardless of the standard version weapon that it is based upon.
Beyond the Octo-Link (GM’s note): Main cannons of sixteen or more fire-linked weapons are possible, but are not
discussed here because weapons of such size in comparison to the ship bearing them make firing them
systemically problematic, owing to their massive energy demands, and so such models are usually considered
experimental prototypes, typically experiencing common issues such as equipment failure and brownouts /
blackouts, which would prove fatal in the field of battle. A GM who wishes to field one is free to devise rules of
their own for it, taking or leaving the above as they see fit.
Power Grid Brownout: Beam weapons draw their power from the starship’s power plant, and a main cannon fired
at full power draws so much of it that the grid browns out for the rest of the round. The ship’s other beam
weapons can still fire that round, but only on a ration chosen by the commander:
Spread: every remaining beam weapon fires at half damage; or
Concentrate: up to half of the ship’s other beam weapons (rounded down) fire at full damage, and the
rest have no available power to fire.
The first beam weapon fired after the main cannon locks in the ration; the two cannot be mixed. (A ship
with only one other beam weapon can fire it only at half damage.) The brownout runs both ways: if any beam
weapon has already fired this round, the main cannon can fire only at 25% or 50% power. A main cannon fired at
25% or 50% power, avoiding the power drain and allowing the ship’s other beam weapons to fire normally.
Projectile weapons carry their own ammunition and missiles carry their own propulsion, so neither draws
on the grid. They fire normally whatever the main cannon does, with one exception: a projectile main cannon is an
electromagnetic accelerator on the same power bus, and at full power it browns out the grid exactly as a beam
main cannon does. Readied attacks and anti-missile autofire made with beam weapons are impacted by the
brownout. However, point-defense systems have their own local power supplies and thus do not.

A missile battery consists of a cluster of up to four identical missile launchers that fire as a single weapon (requiring
643
a single attack roll). Regardless of how many missiles are in the battery, it is considered one size category larger
than the base weapon size, meaning only Colossal (Light) and larger vehicles can bear them. When using battery
fire, every missile after the first in a battery adds a +1 to the threat range for a potential critical, to a maximum of
+3 for a four-missile battery, giving a threat range of 16-20. If the attack succeeds but is not a critical, roll damage
as if one missile hit.
In addition, a missile battery does more damage with a critical hit. For each additional missile in the
battery beyond the first, the critical multiplier of the barrage is increased by 1. For example, a two-missile battery
of plasma missiles (normal multiplier of x2) has a threat range of 18–20 and a critical multiplier of x3, while a four-
missile battery of plasma missiles has a threat range of 18-20 and a critical multiplier of x5. This effect stacks with
other systems that expand a weapon’s critical threat range, such as Achilles targeting software. Also, missile
batteries cannot confirm critical hits against force fields, but they always inflict damage on a per-missile basis to
force fields.
Batteries of missiles cannot be “split” into individual missiles; they either fire all together, or not at all.
Installing missiles in a battery increases the purchase DC of each missile launcher by +2.
Only Colossal (Light) or larger starships can be equipped with missile batteries.
An Example: Arming a TS 7 Cruiser (Mediumweight Colossal Starship)
The scenario is a Tech Scale 7 spacefaring scenario, with the party being the key members of the crew for
the starship enterprising enough to accommodate them. Looking at the Cruiser template, we see that it has
enough room for 8 weapon systems.
First off, for utility’s sake, we say that the Cruiser takes both Grapplers and a Tractor Beam Emitter, to be
able to do whatever it needs to with the objects it encounters in space. That’s two of eight weapons systems.
Striving for versatility in our design, we opt to dedicate two slots to beam weapons, two to missiles, and
two to special weapon types. For our beam weapons, let’s opt for a Heavy Laser, to give the ship some range. The
base Heavy Laser is a Gargantuan weapon doing 10d8 damage and having Purchase DC 31. Twin-linking the
weapon makes it a Colossal (Ultralight) weapon doing 20d8 damage and having Purchase DC 34. Quad-linking it
increases it to a Colossal (Light) 30d8 laser damage weapon having Purchase DC 37. Again, the budget is starting to
get up there, so we’ll take two of these and call them our “phasers”, a portmanteau of “four” and “lasers”.
Our two missile options will both be Plasma missile batteries, each a battery of two Plasma missiles. At a
base cost of Purchase DC 46, as two-missile batteries they’ll increase to Purchase DC 48 each. Their damage does
not change, but their threat range is 18-20, and their critical hit multiplier is x3.
As the first of our special weapons, let’s take an Ion Cannon (10d6 damage, Purchase DC 39, size
Gargantuan). If we upgrade it to a twin-linked Ion Cannon, then its stats become 20d6 damage, Purchase DC 42,
size Colossal (Ultralight). If we upgrade it to a quad-linked Ion Cannon, then it becomes 30d6 damage, Purchase
DC 45, size Colossal (Light). We could upgrade it yet again to a(n octo-linked) Main Cannon inflicting 40d6 Ion
damage, but at Purchase DC 48, and with a main cannon’s claim on the ship’s power grid (see Power Grid
Brownout, above), there might be more efficient ways to spend our money.
Finally, we take a mine layer, with gravitic mines on-hand.
In summation, our enterprising cruiser has Grapplers and a Tractor Beam Emitter, 2 quad-linked “Phaser”
Heavy Lasers, 2 2-missile batteries of plasma missiles, a quad-linked (possibly Main) Ion Cannon, and a mine layer.
We could have built a main cannon (i.e. upgraded one of the beam weapons to an octo-linked weapon or
greater), but the costs can get prohibitive, and our vessel isn’t intended to be a dedicated war machine to that
degree. It can no doubt hold its own in a fight, but it is a space exploration vessel and thus has an array of
concerns to address in equipping itself. This mediumweight cruiser is ready to explore strange new worlds,
seeking out new… well, whatever the captain decides to seek out anew!

Starship Weapon Descriptions
Table: Starship Weapons provides the following statistics for various ranged weapons:
Damage (d, D): The damage the weapon deals in pips and in capital dice (D).
Critical: The critical threat range of the weapon.
Damage Type: Most beam weapons deal a nonspecific type of Energy damage that is only subject to universal
energy resistance. A few weapons deal a specific kind of energy damage: for example, a laser deals Tech Fire
damage. Plasma ignores Hardness. Projectile weapons deal Ballistic damage, which is considered x2 for purposes
of triggering a Massive Damage check, multiplied after any Hardness / Damage Reduction is applied to the damage 645
result, only applicable to targets with a Constitution score of 1 or greater. AA Energy weapons ignore 1D of
Hardness and inflict double damage to force fields. AA Ballistic Weapons ignore 1D of Hardness and automatically
confirm threats to inflict critical damage. Ionic weapons inflict non-lethal damage, ignoring Hardness and dealing
double damage to force fields. Disintegration damage ignores Hardness and inflicts double damage to force fields.
Range Increment: A weapon’s range increment is given in feet. An attack at less than this distance is not penalized
for range. However, each full range increment causes a cumulative –2 penalty on the attack roll. Beam weapons
dissipate and become ineffective past 10 range increments, while projectile weapons have unlimited range. The
number given in brackets is the number of stellar hexes (250’ each) per range increment.
Rate of Fire: Ranged weapons have three possible rates of fire: single shot, semiautomatic, or automatic. A rate of
fire given in brackets is the available rate of fire when that weapon is utilized by a higher TS society, the equivalent
of an advanced version of the weapon.
Single Shot: A weapon with a single shot rate of fire can fire only one shot per attack, even if the gunner has a feat
or other ability that normally allows more than one shot per attack.
Semiautomatic (S): A semiautomatic ranged weapon fires one shot per attack (effectively acting as a single shot
weapon). However, a gunner who gains multiple attacks per round because of his level or because of certain feats
can fire a semiautomatic beam weapon multiple times in rapid succession, getting more than one shot per attack.
Required for feats like Double Tap and Rapid Shot.
Automatic (A): Automatic ranged weapons fire a burst or stream of shots. Only weapons with the automatic rate
of fire can be set on autofire or be used with feats that take advantage of automatic fire (for example, Burst Fire
and Strafe). See Starship Weapons on Autofire for more rules and information.
Minimum Ship Size: The minimum size of starship capable of supporting the weapon.
Purchase DC: The purchase DC of the weapon. The base purchase DC is the cost to build the weapon.
Restriction: The level of license required to purchase the weapon legally. Lic = Licensed (+1 Purchase DC), Res =
Restricted (+2 Purchase DC), Mil = Military (+3 Purchase DC), Ill = Illegal (+4 Purchase DC).
Tech Scale 6 Weapons
Fusion Beam (TS 6): The fusion beam initiates a fusion reaction and then directs the blast at the target. “Fusion” is
what TS 6 calls plasma, as it is a new and difficult technology to utilize, only being available at the starship level.
(10d8 [1d4D] Plasma damage, Crit: 20, RI: 2K ft. [8 hexes], RoF: Single, MSS: Gargantuan, PurDC: 36, Res: Mil)
Gauss Gun (TS 6): The gauss gun is an electromagnetic accelerator that fires tiny ball bearings at an extremely high
velocity. Requiring a momentary recharge of the magnetic capacitors after each shot, this weapon can only fire
single shots. (12d6 [1d4D] Ballistic damage, Crit: 20, RI: 4K ft. [16 hexes], RoF: Single, MSS: Gargantuan, PurDC: 34,
Res: Res)
Laser (TS 6): The simplest beam weapon, the laser is used generally for small craft. It consists of a focused beam of
white-hot light. The laser’s main advantage is the superior range it offers. (8d8 [1d3D] Laser damage, Crit: 20, RI:
5k ft. [20 hexes], RoF: Single/Automatic, MSS: Huge, PurDC: 29, Res: Lic)
Laser, Heavy (TS 6): The heavy laser is simply an oversized laser that pours more energy on the target. Too big to
install on light spacecraft, heavy lasers are common on TS 6 destroyers and larger warships. (10d8 [1d4D] Laser
damage, Crit: 20, RI: 6K ft. [24 hexes], RoF: Single [S/A], MSS: Gargantuan, PurDC: 31, Res: Res)
Mine, Fusion (TS 6): A fusion mine initiates a fusion reaction that deals plasma damage to all starships in its hex

The following devices are commonly used for other purposes on starships, but they can also have applications in
combat, such as holding a ship to expose it to attack or boarding.
Installing one of these systems requires a successful Craft (mechanical) and Craft (electrical) check (DC 30
each) after investing 30 hours. A character without an appropriate tool kit takes a –4 penalty on that skill check. A
starship can have up to two (2) grappling systems, each of which counts as one of the starship’s weapons systems.
Purchase DC: The purchase DC of the system.
Restriction: The level of license required to purchase the system legally.
Grapplers (TS 5)
Grapplers consist of two or more robotic arms fitted with magnetic grips or pads capable of latching onto a single
target, usually another ship. Grapplers can also be used to grab Small or larger objects adrift in space.
Using grapplers against another ship or an unattended object is an attack action. Against another ship, 649
this action provokes an attack of opportunity if the ship being grabbed has a point-defense system. To successfully
grab the target, the starship must first enter the target’s hex; then the starship’s pilot must succeed at a Pilot
check. The Pilot check’s DC depends on the size and Defense of the target being grabbed, as shown on Table:
Grappler Pilot Check DCs below. If the check succeeds, the starship successfully latches onto the target, and the
two ships continue to occupy the same space until the grapplers release their hold. The grappling ship cannot
move as long as it wishes to remain latched and moves in concert with the grappled ship. The larger of the
grappled ships determines their collective course.
As an attack action, a grabbed starship can free itself from a grabbing ship by succeeding at an opposed
Pilot check. Each ship adds a special grapple bonus on its check based on its size: Huge +8, Gargantuan +12,
Colossal +16. A ship may only attempt to free itself once per round.
Grapplers latched onto another ship can release the hold and retract as a free action.

Tractor Beam Emitter (TS 7)
A tractor beam emitter projects a short-range gravitational “tether” that latches onto or immobilizes a single
target, usually a ship or unattended object. The target must be in the same hex or in an adjacent hex.
Using a tractor beam against a starship or an unattended object is an attack action. Against another ship,
this action provokes an attack of opportunity if the ship being grabbed has a point-defense system.
To grab a target with its tractor beam, a starship must succeed at a ranged attack roll. If the attack
succeeds, the smaller ship is immediately pulled into the larger ship’s space (if it isn’t in occupying the same space
already); if both ships are the same size, the target is pulled into the tractoring ship’s space. In any case, being
pulled into another ship’s space by a tractor beam does not count against a ship’s movement. If the tractoring ship
is one or more size categories larger than the target, the target is effectively immobilized, and tractoring ship drags
the target with it when it moves. If the tractoring ship is the same size category as the target or smaller, both the
tractoring ship and the target are effectively immobilized. See the Starship Condition Summary for the effects of
being immobilized.
As an attack action, a tractored starship can free itself from the tractoring ship by succeeding at an
opposed Pilot check. Each ship adds a special grapple bonus on its check based on its size: Colossal (ultralight) +4,
Colossal (light) +8, Colossal (Mediumweight) +12, Colossal (heavy) +16, and Colossal (superheavy) +20. A ship may
only attempt to free itself from a tractor beam (or any other grappling device) once per round. A ship held by
multiple tractor beams may attempt a single grapple check to escape all of the beams, but it must beat the grapple
check results of all opponents.
As a readied action, a ship with a tractor beam emitter can ready the tractor beam to help fend off a
ramming ship. If at the ready and attacked by a ramming attack, the tractor beam emitter operator can make an
opposed attack roll against the ramming ship’s Pilot check to “grab” the ramming ship, reducing the ramming
damage by half (for both the ramming ship and the target). Note that this readied attack will trigger the point-
defense system of the ramming starship, if any.
In most instances (with ships possessing a Class I Sensor system or better), the operator does not have to
declare which enemy ship they are readying for in preparing for an impending ramming attack, as the computer
will warn them of any proximity alert and then the operator can react accordingly. If the tractor beam caught the
ramming ship, then the two ships are tethered by the beam at this point, until one ship or the other breaks the
hold; use the movement rules given above.
A starship using a tractor beam to grab another ship can terminate the beam (thereby releasing its hold 650
on the other ship) as a free action.
Only Colossal ships can be equipped with a tractor beam emitter.
Purchase DC: 15 + one-half the base purchase DC of the starship.
Restriction: Licensed (+1).

Breaking Apart: A starship whose infrastructure has been reduced below 0D but not yet to −½ its maximum IS is
breaking apart. The ship can take no actions, and at the end of each of its turns it loses one-tenth of its maximum
IS (minimum 1D) until it is destroyed or stabilized. The crew may still act aboard: an engineer can stabilize the ship
as a full-round action with a successful Repair check (DC 20), and a ship with a damage control system may
attempt to stabilize as a free action once per round (Repair DC 15), though the system cannot restore IS below 0D.
A stabilized ship stops losing IS but remains disabled and helpless until repaired to 1D IS or better; it begins
breaking apart again if it takes further lethal IS damage. A ship disabled by ionic damage alone is not breaking
apart. Only a nanite repair array can restore a ship below 0D on an automated basis (characters can still conduct
manual repairs) and nothing repairs a destroyed ship (ie. salvage only).
Blinded: A starship whose sensors are damaged or jammed treats every target as having total concealment.
Destroyed: A starship reduced to −½ its maximum IS is destroyed. Nothing repairs a destroyed ship.
Disabled: A starship at 0D IS or less can take no actions, and damage control cannot be performed. It can follow an
autopilot only if its sensors work.
Held / Grappled: A held starship moves in concert with the ship holding it; the larger ship dictates the course. It
takes no move actions of its own (it is carried by the holder), its pilot cannot dodge, and it may attempt to escape
once per round (see Grappling Systems).
Helpless: A starship below 0D IS is helpless: its effective touch AC is 5 + its size modifier.
Immobilized: The starship can take no move actions or pivots and loses its pilot’s Dexterity bonus to touch AC. It
may still attack, but its pilot cannot dodge. It may attempt to escape as described under Grappling Systems.
Ionized: A starship disabled by ionic damage is Disabled until it is de-ionized (see the Hero’s Handbook, p.181). It is
not breaking apart.
Shaken: The crew takes a −2 penalty on attack rolls and checks.

Trained crews suffer a -3 penalty, expert crews suffer a -2 penalty, and ace crews suffer a -1 penalty while zero-
gravity conditions prevail.

The magnetic field is the first primitive energy shield. It uses vast amounts of power to surround the ship with

POINT-DEFENSE SYSTEM (TS 6)
A point-defense system serves two functions: It targets all incoming missiles, and it allows a starship to make at
least one attack of opportunity against every enemy ship passing through its threatened area. The point-defense
system consists of batteries of automated weapons programmed to fire when either of these two conditions is
met. The larger the ship with the point-defense system, and the larger the ship passing through its threatened
area, the more turrets of the point-defense system can be brought to bear against the intruding ship (see below).
A point-defense system does not fire upon mines, cannot be controlled manually by the crew, and cannot
be used to make normal attacks. Only Colossal size starships can have point-defense systems. A point-defense
system requires access to at least one operational sensor system to be usable.
Destroy Missiles: A point-defense system has a 20% chance of destroying any incoming missile (roll once for an
entire missile barrage). A destroyed missile (barrage) deals no damage to the ship.

A starship would be lost in the blackness of outer space without a sophisticated sensor array enabling it to perceive
its surroundings. Sensor arrays allow a starship’s crew to plot safe courses through unexplored star systems, avoid
comets and electromagnetic storms, navigate asteroid belts, analyze planetary surface conditions, detect other
starships nearby, and analyze damage to the ship’s outer hull. Without a functional sensor array, a ship and its
crew are virtually paralyzed.
This section describes several standard sensor arrays. Each sensor array includes a list of functions; each
function requires a move action and a successful Computer Use check (DC 15).
To build a sensor system from scratch, a character must succeed at a Craft (electronic) check (DC 30) after
investing 60 hours in its assembly. A character without an electrical tool kit takes a –4 penalty on the skill check.
The character must spend Wealth equal to the sensor system’s base purchase DC.
Installing a sensor system requires a successful Craft (electrical) check (DC 30) after investing 30 hours. A
character without an electrical tool kit takes a –4 penalty on the skill check.
Different types of sensor systems are detailed below. Note that some other systems (like an auto-pilot
and/or a point-defense system) are dependent on having a sensor system; if the sensors are down, any dependent
systems are unavailable.

The ability to communicate with other ships and bases is vital to starships. The more advanced a ship’s
communications capabilities, the better informed its crew is, and the better they can coordinate with other ships
in the same fleet. Every starship is built with the least expensive communications system available at its Tech
Scale; it occupies no system slot. Better systems are purchased normally.
To build a communication system from scratch, a character must succeed at a Craft (electrical) check (DC
30) after investing a number of hours equal to the ship’s Hit Dice. A character without an electrical tool kit takes a
–4 penalty on the skill check. The character must also spend Wealth equal to the system’s base purchase DC.
Installing a comm system requires a successful Craft (mechanical) check (DC 30) and a successful Craft
(electrical) check (DC 30) after investing 30 hours. A character without a mechanical or electrical tool kit takes a –4
penalty on the appropriate skill check.

Internal Comm Systems
Internal comm systems, though as vital as ship-to-ship communications, are not covered in depth here. Obviously,
the larger a ship’s crew complement, the greater its need for internal communications. The crew must stay in
contact to do their jobs properly. Smaller ships can often get by with headsets jacked into the ship’s network, or
short-range two-way radios, or even just shouting to each other from nearby crew stations. Larger ships require a
more sophisticated system.
A standard internal communication system allows two-way audio communication from any comm station
to any other comm station on the same ship. An internal comm system has a purchase DC based on the ship’s
type: ultralight 13, light 16, mediumweight 19, heavy 22, superheavy 25. Increase the purchase DC by +2 if the
comm stations include video screen displays as well.
RADIO TRANSCEIVER (TS 5)
The radio transceiver can transmit on multiple frequencies in either LOS (line of sight) or omnidirectional mode,
sending messages at the speed of light. A radio transceiver can handle up to ten simultaneous two-way
conversations.
Purchase DC: 21.
LASER TRANSCEIVER (TS 6)
This system uses a beam of coherent light to transmit messages. The laser is unidirectional; the signal cannot be
intercepted or jammed unless it’s beamed directly at a hostile ship or station. However, if the comm officer
doesn’t know exactly where the receiving station is, the laser transceiver is a waste of effort. This has some hidden
drawbacks; a character cannot use the laser transceiver for a general distress call to all stations in the area, for
example. A ship can’t receive laser communications unless it is equipped with the transceiver.
Lasers are limited to the speed of light (8 AU/hour), meaning it can take hours or days to get a response
within a system, or even weeks to get a response at interstellar distances.
Purchase DC: 23.

This massive comm array provides rapid interstellar communications. The array consists of a constellation of
dozens of small transmitters that transmit and receive messages through space at faster-than-light speeds,
enabling communications with a range of 50 light-years.
The signals travel at a rate of 5 light-years per hour. Because of the need for steady signal, the ship must
remain stationary to transmit and receive messages. If the ship moves while its drivesat array is transmitting or
receiving, the ship’s communication officer must make a Computer Use check (DC 30) to avoid losing the signal.
Only mediumweight, heavy, and superheavy ships can be equipped with a drivesat comm array.
Purchase DC: 53.
MASS TRANSCEIVER (TS 7)
This device can transmit instantaneously to any point in the same star system, with no “lag” due to FTS limitations.
However, its range is limited to about 1,000 AU, so the signal can’t cross interstellar space.
Purchase DC: 25.
DRIVE TRANSCEIVER (TS 8)
The drive transceiver is the first interstellar comm system that’s truly practical for small ships or second-rate
colonies. It operates like the much larger TS 7 drivesat comm array, sending a signal up to 50 lightyears distant. The
signal travels at a rate of 5 light-years per hour. The target station must also be equipped with a drive transceiver.
Purchase DC: 28.
ANSIBLE (TS 9)
The ansible is a device that induces precise changes in the energy states of atomic nuclei, without regard to
distance or time. In effect, it permits instantaneous interstellar communications—voice, video, or data transfer—
to any other ship or station equipped with an ansible. Much like a radio, the receiving station has to be attentive to 665
a particular “frequency,” so two ansible-equipped stations must have some prearranged communications
protocols; an ansible cannot pick up any transmissions not intended for that specific frequency.
Purchase DC: 33.

The quality of the crew determines how well a starship performs in and out of combat. Unless otherwise noted,
every starship has a trained crew of nonheroic characters. However, situations could arise where a starship must
rely on an untrained crew. Conversely, expert crews and ace crews are also available—for the right price. Table:
Crew Quality compares four different qualities of crew: untrained, trained, expert, and ace.
Skill Check Modifier: Apply this modifier to all skill checks made by crew.
Pilot’s Dexterity Modifier: A pilot’s Dexterity modifier applies to the starship’s initiative rolls and the starship’s
touch Armor Class.
