classes.d:
The six Hero classes are arguably the most fundamental classes of the game. Based on the six attributes,
the Hero classes have straightforward numbers based on the type of attribute; the physical attribute-based classes
of Strong Hero (Strength), Fast Hero (Dexterity), and Tough Hero (Constitution) have better hit dice and base
attack modifiers but get less skill points than the mental attribute-based classes of Smart Hero (Intelligence), 191
Dedicated Hero (Wisdom), and Charismatic Hero (Charisma). Each Hero class has a skill set that coincides with its
key attribute. Also, choosing the right Starting Occupation can help round out a Hero character’s skill selection.
Hero Hit Base Defense Good Skill

With the best Base Attack progression rate, a Strong Hero is intended for battle, pure and simple.
Their naturally high Strength score lends itself best to melee combat as they get their Strength attribute modifier
to both their melee to-hit rolls and their melee damage rolls. However, at higher levels, the Strong Hero’s ranged
attack modifier will come to equal that of an equivalent-level Fast Hero, even if the Strong Hero has an average
Dexterity, thanks to their superior Base Attack.

The Fast Hero’s attribute is Dexterity, which affects a character’s Armor Class and their ranged attack
rolls. Compounded with their Defense Bonus, Fast Heroes can be very difficult to hit. Similarly, thanks to their high
Dexterity, a Fast Hero is a natural sharpshooter and will likely gravitate to ranged weapons when it comes to
combat.

The Tough Hero has lots of Hit Points, making them natural candidates for frontline combat. Their d10
Hit Die and high Constitution means the Tough Hero will usually have almost twice as many hit points as the
mental-attribute heroes in the party (especially if you use the Heroic Hit Die rule). Some of their Talents can really
augment their staying power too.

The brains of most operations, the Smart Hero usually has several skills maxed out, making them the
authority on said skill within the party. Between the bonus skill points from a high Intelligence and their Savant
starting Talent, it’s not uncommon for a Smart Hero to start out with a total modifier of +10 or more to one or
more skills at first level! But of all the Hero classes, the Smart Hero is the least suited for combat.

What do you think of when you’re told that someone is “dedicated” to something or someone?
The Dedicated Hero is powered by a will that outstrips most others, demonstrated by their high Wisdom score.
They have the best Will saving throws in the party, meaning they will typically resist attempts at mind-control,
manipulation, and magical deception. Such dedication also manifests as a certain zeal on the battlefield with good
Base Attack, Defense Bonus, Fortitude and Will saving throw modifiers.

The Charismatic Hero is all about charm and karma; they have a certain something that people
naturally gravitate to, so much so that even the universe seems to like them. Enjoying better saving throw
modifiers than any other Hero class and starting with more Action Points, the Charismatic Hero has karma pulling
punches for them. The Charismatic Hero’s emphasis is on social skills, such as Bluff, Diplomacy, Intimidate, and
Gather Information, all of which can prove mightier than the sword in the right circumstances.
The nature of your scenario, whether it be physical with lots of combat or cerebral with mysteries and
192
skill-challenges, should take into consideration the composition of your group. The physical-attribute heroes will
excel in combat scenarios, while the mental-attribute characters will see their day in the role-playing and skills-
based scenarios. The best scenarios are those that offer a good mix of both physical and mental action for the PCs.
Hero classes are sometimes accused of being one-dimensional with their focus on a particular attribute, but keep
in mind that Starting Occupations can round out a character, allowing them to access skills their Hero class doesn’t
normally offer.

As mentioned earlier, the Basic classes are considered “basic” because they can be taken as soon as 1st
level character, and they allow progression from 1st level all the way to 20th level, allowing the character to stay
single-classed throughout their progression, keeping things “basic”. In many if not most cases, player characters
end up multiclassing, usually progressing from a Hero class or a Basic class into one (or more) Advanced class(es) or
Prestige class(es). However, if a player wanted to keep it simple, the simplest character to make would be a Basic
class character who never multiclasses. Most Basic classes offer increasingly exceptional class features at the upper
levels, so there are unique rewards for building such single-classed characters.

In many ways the Aristocrat is like the Charismatic Hero, with a focus on the social skills. However,
thanks to a formal education the Aristocrat has access to a wide array of Knowledge skills too, and they start with
almost all the same combat feats as a Fighter (although neither the Base Attack nor the Hit Die). Of note is their
Influence ability; always use this as a tool to enhance the scenario, and never let the player leverage it against you
to get access to items or powers out of turn, nor as a scenario-avoiding solution (i.e., getting someone else to do
the mission and bring the treasure back to the Aristocrat). Powerful items are always in high demand and thus are
either outright unavailable or they get noticed when they move in the market, drawing unwanted attention from
the authorities and/or other (unsavory) contenders for the same power. Influence should be exactly that; a
positive influence on how the game progresses, not a game-breaker.

The Bard is a consummate jack-of-all-trades, offering good Base Attack and Defense Bonus progression, a
select list of arcane spells (if yours is an Arcane Scale 1 or higher scenario) that also includes magical healing (!),
excellent Reflex and Will saves, and their own special brand of magic known as Bardic Music! They also have a
well-rounded skill list with good skill point progression, and their Bardic Knowledge ability gives them a chance to
know valuable tidbits or clues about the scenario. Their only drawback? They’ve been stereotyped in pop culture
as incessantly attempting to seduce every sentient being they meet; unless you’re playing a parody-style game do
NOT let your Bard PCs do such things, always force them to role-play it, and give a corresponding circumstance
modifier (anywhere for +100 for being on par with the storyline to -100 for being ridiculous or insulting). However,
the Bard can be so much more than “the good-looking one” of the party when played properly. The class also
offers a non-magic variant if the player wishes and the GM allows.

With their d12 Hit Die and their Rage ability augmenting their Strength and Constitution for combat,
Berserkers are pound-for-pound the toughest Basic class. They have the best Base Attack progression but only fair
Defense Bonus progression, as defense is not a Berserker’s strong suit. They are one of the simplest classes
available, offering little in the way of customization, focused purely on aggression in combat. The Berserker is for
the player who wants combat and doesn’t want to overthink it.

A priest or devotee of their god or principle(s), a Cleric has access to divine magic and the special ability to
Turn / Rebuke Undead (depending on whether they’re good or evil). Like the Dedicated Hero, the Cleric offers a
good average across the spectrum of defensive and offensive capabilities. The Cleric’s claim to fame is their ability
to heal with divine magic, making them a staple of almost every fantasy roleplaying group. While the Druid loses
the ability to Turn Undead, their other abilities in nature mastery and their ability to Wildshape (Shapechange into
Animal forms) more than makes up for it in the long run. Alongside the Psion and the Wizard, the Cleric is arguably
one of the most powerful classes in the game once it gains access to 9th-level spells at 17th level.
193

As the name suggests, the Expert is someone who outstrips their peers when it comes to expertise in one
or more skills. The Expert is not a combat class per se, but with their superior access to Expert skills, which include
vehicle combat feats, and the Cybertaker feat, one might argue that an Expert is just as good as or better than a
Fighter in being a combat pilot or cyborg. More times than not, however, the Expert is “dipped” into as a
supplemental class, with characters taking a few levels to get access to some additional Expert feats, exactly
because the character wants to go into artificing, piloting, or cybernetic augmentation. Taken to higher levels, the
Expert’s ability to build items can become revolutionary in game terms, eventually gaining access to technology
from the next higher Tech Scale! Of course, by that point they will have earned it.

Of all the Basic classes, the Fighter is the most customizable combat class; the Berserker relies on raw
aggression, while the Ranger has a specialty terrain and favored enemy. With a Fighter feat every other level,
above and beyond the regular progression of gaining a feat every three levels, the Fighter class encompasses a
broad range of possible fighting styles. Many combat-oriented characters will take a few levels in Fighter to grab
up a few Fighter feats and superior Base Attack modifiers. The dedicated Fighter character, although rare, is a
sight to behold in combat, forcing many GMs to adapt to their combat style accordingly.

Mainly intended for the empty-handed martial artist, the Monk has an eclectic array of combat and buff
abilities. They are built to be self-sufficient, with natural attacks that become magical in nature and supernatural
capabilities like the ability to Abundant Step (aka Dimension Door) and deliver the dreaded Quivering Palm (a
delayable death attack). Of all the Basic classes, the Monk class might be considered the most context-specific,
and thus the most optional, depending on the scenario.

If divine power is permitted in your scenario, and your group is largely Good in alignment / allegiance,
then there may be a Paladin in your group. With a warrior’s Base Attack and Hit Die, but also with divine spells and
abilities to boot, the Paladin is a great frontline addition to any group. Of course, the alignment restriction (i.e.,
Lawful/Good only) can make for some stringent roleplaying on the player’s part, and thus the Paladin may not be
right for your group if the scenario involves any grey- or black-market activities that would violate their Lawful
sensibilities. An agreeable player can opt to “play dumb” and make a point of looking the other way, but obvious
and overt violations of fair and just laws such as “don’t steal” and “don’t murder” cannot be tolerated by a true
Paladin. Of course, a wise paladin will not jump to blows but rather use a measured response such as seeking
explanations and giving reprimands in a desire for possible repentance and forgiveness. However, there are limits
to what even the most merciful Paladin can accept before they will feel a stand must be taken in the name of the
moral principles being violated.

The most psychically powerful of the psionic classes, a properly-built Psion can rival any Cleric or Wizard in
terms of power, gaining access to the most powerful 9th-level powers at 17th level. There are six major Disciplines
available to the Psion, granting access to specialized powers no other classes can take (at least, not without the
Expanded Knowledge feat). However, they start out quite weak with only a few powers and a d4 Hit Die.
Furthermore, their powers are relatively few in comparison to the Cleric’s list or Wizard’s spellbook, such that
choosing the wrong powers can severely hamper a Psion’s ability to keep up with the power scale of the party.
Consider allowing a Psion character to select a different power if you find that a current selection is getting little to
no usage. Like other psionic classes, two great advantages of the Psion is their ability to manifest their powers
without display (see the Concentration skill), allowing them to hide the source of their fearsome manifestations
when used in public or under scrutiny, and the ability to use any of their powers whenever they wish on demand
(as long as they have the required power points to manifest the power), unlike the Cleric and the Wizard who must
allot their spell selections at the beginning of each day.

A tracker and survivalist, the Ranger is a useful member of any group ranging in the wild. Their Base
Attack progression makes them relevant in combat, even more so if they happen to be fighting a favored enemy.
An animal companion is always handy for keeping watch or being able to go where the characters cannot, and if
the scenario offers divine magic then the Ranger’s access to Druid spells will likewise prove handy. Eventually the
Ranger develops a favored terrain, which you should discuss with the player as to what options might be
194
reasonable, based both on the character’s past experiences and the GM’s likely plotline, to ensure a choice of
favored terrain that is both justifiable and useful.

The Rogue is a specialist in cloak-and-dagger operations, with a focus on Dexterity- and Charisma-based
skills, and a lot of skill points to make sure they’re good at them. Their Trapfinding ability sets the Rogue apart
when it comes to exploring trapped areas, and with their Sneak Attack ability, Rogues are useful in combat, but on
a complementary basis; they need a primary attacker to help them flank their target. Although they might enjoy a
half-decent Armor Class thanks to a high Dexterity, the lack of heavy armor and d6 Hit Die mean the Rogue is
usually not up for many heavy blows.

Only available in scenarios offering divine magic, the Saint is a direct representative of a deity, and as such
has certain power-scale and role-playing considerations. The Saint’s innate access to their deity’s power means
several starting Domain powers, but their spell list ends up being very specific according to their deity’s spheres of
power. At the highest levels, the Saint gains the ability to perform a Miracle daily, and they gain access to some
9th-level spells. However, they necessarily serve their god’s agenda (whether directly or indirectly is the GM’s
choice) and are the same alignment as their god. Like the Paladin and Cleric, deviations from their deity’s dictates
will see them excommunicated, losing all their divine abilities.
As an option, if a Saint falls from grace for some reason yet continues to live, there is a small chance
(GM’s choice) that a diametrically opposed deity of the opposite alignment will offer the fallen Saint an
opportunity for apostasy. If the ex-Saint chooses apostasy, they become an Apostate of their former deity, now
dedicated to the destruction of their former church. The new Apostate immediately changes alignments and
effectively becomes a Saint of their new diametrically opposed deity, gaining access to the Domains of their new
deity, and choosing their spells with the objective of destroying their former church. Although the Apostate need
not immediately seek the destruction of their former church, all their actions must be to somehow further their
efforts in attempting to do so.

One of the most powerful classes at higher levels, the Sorcerer is initially one of the weakest. With a
narrow selection of spells and a d4 Hit Die, the Sorcerer cannot fight for long before they need to rest, at least at
lower levels. However, once they reach 6th level and access to 3rd-level spells, the balance is restored, until by 10th
level they are beginning to have a greater impact on the scenario than other equivalent level characters. While
they don’t have the range of spellcasting options of a Wizard, their innate ability to select whatever spells they
want as they progress means they have access to the spells they want as soon as they qualify for them, unlike the
Wizard who must find their spells to add to their spellbook first. Also, the ability to spontaneously cast means they
always have access to any and all of their spells on demand, as long as they have the spell points to cast the spell.
Used properly, the Sorcerer’s familiar greatly enhances their utility and survivability in the early levels.

A balanced class with combat and psionic options, the Warmind is a solid frontline member of any
party. Although they don’t technically have the Base Attack progression of a combat class, the Warmind more
than makes up for it with powers that augment their offensive and defensive capabilities. Also, the feats offered
by the class allow it to mix and match Fighter feats and Power feats for a personalized combat style. However, the
division in their studies between the physical and the mental means they only progress up to 6th-lvl psionic powers
over the course of 20 levels.

The Wilder is a psionic powered by emotions, their powers augmented by wild surges and the euphoria
caused by channeling such power. Although sturdier than the Psion, having a d6 Hit Die and the intuitive ability to
Evade Touch, the Wilder has a narrower selection of psionic powers than a Psion has, because Wilders don’t have
access to Discipline powers (at least not without the Expanded Knowledge feat). A Wilder can entertain the notion
of toe-to-toe fighting, but usually in a supporting role, at least in the early levels. With powers ranging up to
mightiest 9th-level powers as of 18th-level Wilder, they rank amongst the most powerful classes in the late game.

The Wizard starts out physically weak, with d4 Hit Die, no armor proficiencies, and only a few spells
known. However, they evolve quickly, until by 5th level they can hold their own with access to 3rd-level spells, by
9th level they can teleport, and as of 17th level they have access to the most-powerful 9th-level spells, up to and
195
including Wish, making them one of the most powerful classes in the game. The Wizard’s edge lies in their
spellbook; a Wizard can have access to as many spells as they can find to add to their repertoire, and thus they
tend to form guilds, to both gain access to spells through trade while controlling access to other spells through
regulations. Like the Sorcerer, the Wizard can opt to gain a familiar, an intelligent pet and companion to help them
survive the early stages of the game, even if only an extra set of eyes and ears to start.
Despite being “basic” in nature, not every Basic class is suited to every scenario (for example, the Monk
class). If a Basic class doesn’t work for your scenario, then don’t allow it. Keep in mind that you as the GM are
always the final arbiter on what is or is not permissible, regardless of whether the class is “Basic”. Similarly, some
Basic classes are going to be ruled out by the nature of your scenario and the Six Scales you’ve assigned to it
(Arcane Scale, Divine Scale, Psionic Scale, etc.).

An Advanced Class is considered “advanced” because of the multiclassing component; the character must
have “advanced” to the appropriate level to qualify for the class, and the management of a multiclassed character
might be considered an “advanced” level of gameplay. While the rules for multiclassing are straightforward,
players still have to make sure their characters have the prerequisites to be able to progress in their desired
Advanced Class(es), as well as keep track of their aggregate modifiers. All Advanced Classes offer 10 levels of
advancement.

Something of a niche class, the Ace Pilot specializes in riding, driving, or piloting a mount or vehicle. If
your scenario is a tight-space underground dungeon crawl, an Ace Pilot is going to have limited applicability
(perhaps a power armor pilot?). However, in many scenarios Ace Pilots have their place, charging their steed
defiantly into the jaws of death, or piloting their mecha or starcraft into the thick of battle. Fast Heroes, Experts,
and Rogues make up the majority of Ace Pilots.

The Ambassador is almost entirely a role-playing class, usually involved in the high art of diplomacy
and statecraft. If your scenario is going to be mostly battle or isolated from the perks of civil society, then an
Ambassador may prove of limited use. However, if your scenario involves politics and intrigue, then the
Ambassador is a handy addition to the party, with a network of contacts able to help them in their cause.
Charismatic Heroes, Aristocrats, and sometimes Bards or Experts (in Diplomacy) are the most common candidates
for Ambassadors.

A Bodyguard is a solid addition to any team, with a d12 Hit Die and a unique class ability that allows
them to step into “Harm’s Way” for a nearby team member. Of course, they are putting themselves in danger in
the process, and thus being a Bodyguard is a high-risk occupation, but done properly it can be very rewarding. In
scenarios where there is no immediate or evident threat, a Bodyguard may prove to be more of a tag-along role.
Tough Heroes, Fighters (Berserkers tend to lose their cool) with a tendency for self-sacrifice, and Paladins usually
go on to be Bodyguards.

When you’re playing a scenario with no divine magic, and thus no Clerics or Saints, then the
Combat Medic will be the party’s healer. With a focus on the Treat Injury skill, the Combat Medic eventually
reaches a point where they can perform a Medical Miracle, capable of bringing back characters who are otherwise
statistically dead! Even if the scenario isn’t combat-oriented, the Combat Medic has access to some useful skills.
Dedicated Heroes and Experts most commonly demonstrate the focus required to become Combat Medics.

Whether it be a professional stuntman or an extreme parkour practitioner, the Daredevil pushes their
feats of agility to the limit. They gravitate naturally to Driving, Piloting, and Tumbling thanks to their Growing
Confidence class ability, and their ability at higher levels to shrug off damage and effects can make them difficult
foes to contend with. Fast Heroes, Rogues, and other Dex-based classes make the best Daredevils.
196

An Explorer comes in many forms; the intrepid archaeologist, the itinerant philosopher, or the world-
savvy wanderer. The one thing they all have in common is an unquenchable thirst for knowledge and a knack for
getting by. Their Explorer Lore ability is near-identical to the Bardic Knowledge ability, and equally useful, giving
the GM a way in which to offer hooks and clues to the PCs when needed. Any character with the right Starting
Occupation can be an Explorer.

The Field Officer is one who specializes in leadership on the battlefield, guiding their companions to
victory through strategy and fervor. Their ability to give out modifiers in combat allows a party to be greater than
the sum of its parts, and a properly played Field Officer can enhance a group to perform significantly better than
their average character level would suggest; be forewarned, GMs! Charismatic Heroes and characters with a
penchant for tactics (as in the Knowledge skill) can make effective Field Officers.

Probably the “sneakiest” of the Advanced classes, the Infiltrator specializes in those Dex- and Cha-
based skills that allow them to break and enter wherever required. From Disable Device to Disguise, the Infiltrator
has the skillset to penetrate the enemy’s fortress. They are geared towards finesse rather than fighting, but their
tendency to be able to Tumble and their superior Defense Bonus both offer them some staying power.
Charismatic Heroes, Bards, and Rogues tend towards the art of the Infiltrator.

An Investigator is someone dedicated to finding out the truth. Although each Investigator has their
own motivations, their methods are remarkably similar, using their skills and their class ability to Profile their
targets, finding out what others want hidden. They are invaluable in whodunit scenarios or ones with political
intrigue, but they are only fair to middling in combat scenarios. Dedicated Heroes, Clerics, and Paladins most
commonly become Investigators.

For the character who wants to harness the power afforded by money, the Marketeer is an ideal class
choice. Their emphasis is in Cha-based skills, with a good cross-section of Int- and Wis-based skills to round out
their business acumen. As one might expect, the Marketeer is not an ideal combat class, but they usually have
enough money for a Bodyguard or two! Charismatic Heroes, Aristocrats, and Rogues sometimes go the way of the
Marketeer.

The generic term for one who focuses on self-mastery to become a living weapon, a Martial Artist
is obviously a combat class. Depending on one’s focus in the physical attributes, a character may practice a “hard”
martial art using Strength and strikes, or a “soft” martial art using Dexterity and avoiding the enemy’s strikes.
Physical-attribute Heroes, Fighters, and other warrior types usually gravitate to this class.

The penultimate role-playing class, the Personality is all about Charisma, wowing others with their
presence. Usually an actor, an artist, or other public performer, the Personality is not well-geared towards
combat, so combat-heavy campaigns won’t be ideal scenarios for a Personality. However, in sessions with lots of
social interaction and/or political intrigue, the Personality is right up there with the Ambassador in terms of “soft
power”, capable of influencing powerful members of the elite through favors and guile. Charismatic Heroes,
Bards, and some Experts tend to establish cults of Personality.

As the name suggests, the Sharpshooter is a master of the ranged attack. Usually specializing in a
particular ranged weapon, their bonuses can get quite substantial, allowing them to hit the most evasive
opponents. The Sharpshooter negates the usual weakness for trying to use a ranged weapon in melee combat, but
they don’t threaten neighboring hexes with their ranged weapon, so they don’t get attacks of opportunity. Fast
Heroes, Fighters, Rangers, and Rogues are the most common classes to go into Sharpshooter.

The Soldier is a professional warrior, one who battles for a living. They always have a weapon of choice,
and they become very effective with that weapon as they progress in the Soldier class. They have a better Reflex
save than the Fighter, and gain abilities at higher levels that Fighters don’t, such as offering Tactical Aid to their
unit and being able to Walk It Off, allowing them to withstand withering punishment. Physical-attribute Heroes
and warrior types make up the bulk of Soldiers.
197

The Survivor does exactly that; survive. The class is geared towards developing superior defenses, but it
eventually allows for flashes of offensive prowess with its “Fight or Flight” and “Best Defense” class abilities, both
acquired by 5th level. Even one level of Survivor gives a nice bump to a character’s saving throws and defense
bonus, with either Evasion or Improved Evasion (if the character already had Evasion before taking 1st level
Survivor). Fast Heroes, Dedicated Heroes, and Tough Heroes tend to be Survivors.

The Tactician is the formal student of war, one who makes their mind their greatest weapon. As one can
imagine, the tactical options available to the Tactician can be overwhelming for a novice player, but when played
properly, a sufficiently smart Tactician can risk going toe-to-toe with almost any adversary! As Intelligence is the
driving attribute behind this class, Smart Heroes, Experts, Psions, and Wizards are the most prone to develop one
or more levels in Tactician.

For the character who likes toys, the Techsmith is their go-to class. Focusing on any and all of the skills
associated with creating items, a good Techsmith will ensure the party has all the latest gadgetry. Item creation
can make or break your game, so be careful about what you allow. Typically, items from the same Tech Scale as
the scenario are fine, but the highest level Techsmiths can build Prototypes of technology from the next Tech
Scale, which can be akin to magic items! Smart Heroes and Experts most commonly delve into the arts of the
Techsmith.

The Weaponmaster focuses all their development into the mastery of one weapon. They can
become fearsome warriors, with an array of bonuses and abilities that can dominate the battle scene. However,
their single-minded focus can leave them lacking in social and utility skills, which is something to keep in mind
when creating scenarios involving Weaponmaster PCs. Physical-attribute Heroes and warrior-type classes will be
the most likely to embrace the path of the Weaponmaster.
Just as the Hero classes are meant to cover off the basics, the Advanced classes are meant to offer an
array of the most common adventuring types found in gaming and literature. Running the gamut from heavy role-
playing to purely combat, the Advanced classes allow characters to specialize in a certain forte, hopefully one
that’s well-suited to your scenario and/or campaign. Unlike Prestige classes, which can be extraordinarily powerful
or specific in their application, the Advanced classes are general enough in nature that they should be applicable to
almost any scenario.
Of course, some scenarios are going to be heavy in one aspect or the other (i.e., role-playing or combat),
and for PCs focused on the other end of the spectrum, they may find themselves relegated to a secondary or
spectator role in the meantime. With proper management of expectations, players will realize that this is a part of
the game and be gracious about it. However, even the most patient player will grow bored if they have nothing to
do for too long. In these cases, try to either give them a subsidiary role that continues to involve them, or “pan”
back and forth between PCs to keep everyone involved.

Where Hero, Basic, and Advanced classes are intended to cover off the most common adventuring paths,
Prestige classes offer nuanced benefits that can make or break a scenario. For this reason, they are called
“Prestige” classes, because they necessarily require the “prestige” of the GM’s approval in order to be played
(technically, every class requires the GM’s permission, but arguably the Hero, Basic, and Advanced classes are
common enough to be considered “pre-approved” in a manner of speaking). Some Prestige classes offer
incredible power (especially those geared towards magic and psionics) and need to be carefully considered. The
prerequisites set for each Prestige class are a benchmark to help gauge when a PC is ready for such power, and as
such the prerequisites should not be casually disregarded. Below is a synopsis of the Prestige classes available in
the E&E GM’s Guide and things to consider when approving them.
Anti-Hero: One of the few Prestige classes that can be taken at 1st level (the others being the Elementalist and the
Heavy), Anti-Hero is a Prestige class due to the unique roleplaying situations it can bring to the table. Neither
198
bound to good nor evil, the Anti-Hero is capable of morally questionable acts in the name of “vengeance” or
“justice” that Heroes typically won’t commit. They also have some unique rules around the use of Action Points
that a GM would want to be aware of before permitting. The Anti-Hero can be a fun class that allows both combat
and role-playing in the right circumstances; just make sure those circumstances prevail before permitting one in
your scenario.

One of the most difficult Prestige classes to get into, if not one of the most powerful, is the Archmage.
This Prestige class offers a Wizard or Sorcerer who is already capable of 7th-level spells even more power! As 7th-
level spells aren’t acquired until 13th level Wizard or 14th level Sorcerer, the Archmage is a rarely-witnessed
Prestige class, and for good reason; the power they wield can influence the fates of nations and worlds. If you’re
prepared to adjudicate an Arcane Scale 5 or higher scenario and permit the use of 5th-9th level spells, then the
Archmage is a logical step in the progression of the high-level Wizard or Sorcerer.

The Artificer specializes in building magic and/or psionic items. If your scenario uses or permits such
items, then the Artificer should be a permissible Prestige class. Just keep in mind that an Artificer in the party can
mean lots of magic / psionic items for the party, which can tip the balance of power if not managed properly. For
example, powerful items should require special reagents that can’t simply be bought on the market and must be
found. Also, be sure to enforce the time and XP requirements for building such items so that Artificers must be
selective in what they build based on said constraints.

Besides the Super-Villain, the Assassin is the only other Prestige class that requires an Allegiance to or
Alignment of Evil, and rightly so; the Assassin is a contract killer, and as such sees people only as potential marks.
Once an Assassin is in the party, no one, PC or NPC alike, is safe. Their ability to justify killing and murder can derail
sessions and create out-of-control scenarios when the wrong person is killed for the wrong reasons. Unless you
are running a sandbox scenario where the PCs are dictating the course of action (i.e., no prepared sessions, just on-
the-fly storytelling), or your scenario specifically involves the storyline of an assassin, you should carefully consider
whether or not you will allow this Prestige class. More likely, such a Prestige class will be used as an antagonist by
the GM.

The Bloodluster lets the exultation of battle take them to a new level, one where thought and feeling
become one, and thus Berserkers and Wilders are almost exclusively the only stock Bloodlusters come from. As
the height of their power only comes in the fury of battle, Bloodlusters are combat-heavy classes. Their class
abilities only augment what the Berserker and/or the Wilder class brings to the table; the Bloodluster is a
straightforward class that likely doesn’t threaten to break your game, but can be a lot of fun to see in action,
especially the Berserker / Wilder dual-classed version.

The zealous holy warrior who serves the agenda of their deity, the Crusader is typically a Paladin or Saint
who has thrown themselves into proselytizing for their faith. As such they have a heavier roleplaying component
than their prerequisite class, with the ability to convert NPCs to their deity’s following. Just keep in mind that in
the case of either the Proselytize or Mass Appeal ability, it takes 10 minutes to complete the conversion. This
means that, typically speaking, only Neutral or friendlier NPCs will take the time to hear the Crusader out. With
good modifiers across the board, the Crusader is a solid addition to any group (if you can bear their constant
sermons!).

The Ecclesiarch is a font of divine power, capable of miracles in the name of their god. Only available
in Divine Scale 5 or higher scenarios, the Ecclesiarch is a Cleric or Saint with the full support of their church in the
pursuit of their deity’s agenda. If you have an Ecclesiarch in your party, know that the party will have little to fear
from injury or death. Sometimes to balance the scales, the opposing alignment’s church will seek to answer any
action on the Ecclesiarch’s part; keep this in mind when considering adversaries for the party.

One who dabbles in swords and sorcery, the Eldritch Knight is a great frontline addition to any
party. Their ability to participate in a stand-up fight, along with the array of options offered to them by their
199
spellcasting, Eldritch Knights are handy in almost any encounter. Even better, the Knight who goes to 10th level in
this Prestige class is formally knighted, which comes with its own perks, especially if the character has an
Allegiance to a group or organization that will support the Knight’s claim.

Either through magic or mutation, the Elementalist is one who specializes in harnessing the power of
one of the four basic elements; earth, air, water, or fire. Each one has the advantages of the element to which
they are attuned, such as great strength and durability for Vitrolians (earth), electric bolts and flight for Ambrians
(air), extreme cold and fluid form for Kryonians (water), and bolts of fire and a sheath of flame for Vesuvians (fire).
Being focused in their element, Elementalists can sometimes find themselves at a disadvantage when an
encounter doesn’t play to their strength (for example, an aerial battle with a Vitrolian involved), but by and large
they are useful in a fight.

The Elocater is a master of space (and by association, time), capable of traveling great distances with a
thought. Their focus on mobility is their chief advantage in combat, able to easily maneuver to flank opponents
and capable of a quick retreat if the battle suddenly turns on them. Even better, the Elocater is not solely about
mobility, and with their other powers they can ensure they’re well-rounded to be able to do more than just get
around quickly.

Whether magic or psionic in nature, the Guildmember’s strength is the same; the power offered to
them by their Guild. The most obvious advantage is their Membership with the Guild, allowing them access to
spells / powers that they don’t have themselves. This offers great versatility in terms of the wide array of spells /
powers available to the Guildmember, capable of retrieving a spell/power from the Guild as their circumstances
dictate. Once a Guildmember reaches Guildmaster at 10th level, their breadth of power is virtually unmatched.
Note that the opposite side of the coin when it comes to being a Guildmaster (10th-level Guildmember) is
that the character’s rank and status are also known to their enemies, and every guild has enemies! Rival guilds,
diametrically opposed orders and evil churches dedicated to death and/or destruction seek the information and
power the guild offers, and the character is just one more way to try and get those secrets. Although not officially
the case, almost always a new Guildmaster finds themselves on a different scale of political intrigue, one that
typically results in deadly traps and ambushes in attempts to rob or kill this new piece on the grand chessboard.

The colloquial term for a heavy conversion cyborg, the Heavy is a character with lots of cybernetic
implants. This means they can have a wide array of sensors and/or weapons, depending on their creator, but they
all have Heavy Subcutaneous Armor, giving them great staying power in combat with their additional Hardness and
Hit Points. For this reason, most “Heavies” are combat-oriented, and with several melee and ranged weapons in
their built-in arsenal, they are a welcome addition to any party’s frontline.
The Heavy is the futuristic equivalent of the Berserker, insofar as their combat options are typically
straightforward and intended to inflict lots of damage. Some Heavy characters will have cybernetic tricks up their
sleeve like poison dispensers and/or nonlethal takedown methods such as manacles or tasers. But would a Heavy
really be a heavy infantry unit without one or more heavy weapons?

The divine equivalent of the Eldritch Knight, the Holy Knight studies the arts of war and their deity’s
tenets in equal measure. Any class with access to divine spells can multiclass into Holy Knight, but the majority of
those referred to as Holy Knights are Clerics or Saints with a predilection for combat. Paladins and Rangers can
become Holy Knights as well, but they surrender their more nuanced class progression for straight spell
progression and the occasional feat selection; consider carefully whether the original Basic class or the Holy Knight
class serves the player’s objectives before advising a Paladin or Ranger character to become a Holy Knight. Like the
Eldritch Knight, the 10th level Holy Knight attains Knighthood, a worthwhile consideration in most campaigns.

Known interchangeably as a Seer or Sage, the Loremaster is a specialist in information, and if
“knowledge is power” then the properly-played Loremaster can prove very powerful indeed! A Loremaster is
incredibly handy for finding information the party needs for their quest. Whether it’s the existence or location of a
legendary artifact, or an obscure but critical piece of information regarding an enemy, the Loremaster has a good
chance of knowing it or learning it for the party. Arcane types gravitate to this class, as it allows them to continue
200
their studies unabated (i.e., no levels where spell capabilities don’t improve).

The pinnacle of mental prowess, the Metamind offers a specialized niche for each of the Disciplines,
including the Monad (Psychoportation), the Precog (Clairsentience), the Physical Phoenix (Metacreativity), the
Telekinetic Terror (Psychokinesis), the Telepathic Tyrant (Telepathy), and the Uncarnate (Psychometabolism). If a
character in your group qualifies for Metamind, be sure to know exactly which Mental Mastery powers they select
so that you can be ready for them in your scenario, because they can be real game-changers! This class is the
exclusive territory of Psions and Wilders.

Possessing two variations, the worldly “Planetstrider” and the otherworldly “Planestrider”, this class
is typically an evolution of a Ranger, although the potential prerequisite of being able to Plane Shift means psionic
and magic variants also happen. Offering a good base attack progression and balanced saving throw modifiers, the
Planestrider learns ever-greater means by which to weather the elements, no matter where they travel to. The
Planestrider is a well-weathered traveler and hardy addition to any party, with specialty areas that will make them
especially useful in certain scenarios.

A computer specialist only prevalent in Tech Scale 5 and later scenarios, the Shadowjack is
sometimes equated with the Cleric in terms of importance in futuristic settings. The ability to control software and
computerized resources is often invaluable in translating into success for hi-tech missions. Whether it’s hacking or
preventing oneself from getting hacked, the Shadowjack can get you into whatever you need, virtually speaking. Of
course, as armchair warriors, they do not make the best frontline fighters. Rogues and Experts are usually
precursor classes to the budding Shadowjack.

The Soulstalker is the penultimate tracker, possessing a unique “Soulsight” to track their targets
unerringly. With a focus on finding their quarry, the Soulstalker has a select cadre of powers enabling them to
track targets through space and time. At higher levels the Soulstalker even develops the ability to dimensionally
corner their mark(s), until the greatest Soulstalkers, who can read the mind of their target like a book. A great
character for gathering intel and being able to hold their own in combat, the vast majority of Soulstalkers come
from Psychic Warriors, although other rarer career paths are possible.

A technologically developed Mutant, a Splice gains access to Mutation Points to buy heightened attributes,
advantages, and even super-powers! If you have Splices in your scenario then you are playing a Mutation Scale 1
or higher scenario, and you hopefully know what you’re in for! The Mutation Point system is the most open-ended
character design possibility in E&E, and thus the one most capable of abuse. Hopefully ingenuity will win out over
munchkinism, but ultimately, if a player threatens to develop a character that will break the game, then feel free
to nerf it. Since a character only has to be tough enough (i.e., Con 13+) to survive the gene therapy sessions to
become a Splice, this class can be dipped into by any sufficiently tough PC.
Super-Hero / Super-Villain: Arguably the quintessential Prestige class for any “super-power” based scenario, the
Super-Hero is a natural step in the progression of any super-powered Hero class character. Indeed, if one or more
characters in your group are running a Super-Hero, you should seriously consider creating a Super-Villain to
oppose them; the special abilities specific to counter Super-Hero characters will make your villain a memorable
one! Again, since Mutation Points are involved, watch out for game-breaking combos (or better yet, feel free to
develop a few yourself if that’s how your players want it!).

The arcane side and the psionic side of the same coin, this class specializes in the
combination of technology and magic / psionics. Capable of invoking supernatural control over machines, the
Technomage / Technopath is a revered character in hi-tech scenarios. They can near-instantly repair weapons and
armor, making them invaluable on any battlefield. These characters are specialized towards technology, not unlike
the Shadowjack, however their specialty does have applications in combat, making them more effective against
mecha and hi-tech opponents.

This kind of Trickster takes trickery to the next level, relying on (either magical or psychic) telekinesis to
201
pull off the truly impossible! Whether it’s picking locks and pockets up to 30 feet away or attacking opponents
telekinetically from the opposite angle, the Trickster is one class that doesn’t let the enemy see ‘em coming.
Arcane and psychic rogue-types gravitate toward this class, owing to its reliance on the supernatural to perform
otherwise-impossible tricks.
A Final Note on Prestige Classes
Prestige classes offer some of the most powerful abilities in the game. If you feel or discover that a certain
class or ability is detracting from your game, consider changing it. Insofar that it is a player’s character we’re
talking about, and likely a power or ability that enticed the player to play that class in the first place, approach the
player diplomatically and in private to discuss how the ability in question is compromising your game, and what
options the two of you can explore to change things fairly but ultimately for the best. Perhaps let the player
suggest an alternate power or ability to replace the one being modified, or collaborate on how to modify it (i.e.,
“nerf it”) to restore balance to your game.

Facings for Weapons and Shields
If desired for an even grittier tactical feel, the areas that weapons can be used to attack and that shields
can be used to defend are dependent on the hand / limb holding the weapon or shield. If a weapon is held in the
right hand, it can be used to attack any target within its threatened area on the right side of it or in front of it. If a
weapon is held in the left hand, it can be used to attack any target within its threatened area on the left side of it
or in front of it. Similarly for a shield, the shield’s bonus to AC can be used against any attack from the same side
202
as the shield or from the front of the bearer.
If using this rule, the feat Weapon Focus should allow the weapon to be used on the opposite flank as well
(so if the weapon is being held in the right hand it can be used to attack a target on the left side, and vice versa).
Similarly, the feat Shield Parry should allow the shield to be used on the opposite flank to defend its bearer.
Hex Grid with Associated Flanks and Firing Arcs (North-South)
This is based on a Medium-sized Creature / Ultralight Starship 1-Hex scale. Blue and green hexes: can
attack, and be attacked from, the Front / Fore; yellow with adjoining green and orange hexes: can attack, and be
attacked from, the Left / Port or Right / Starboard, as appropriate; red and orange hexes: can attack, and be
attacked from, the Rear / Aft. These are the firing arcs for a creature / vehicle / mecha / starship facing north; just
flip the grid configuration when facing south.
Here is the hex grid configuration for firing arcs based on a creature / vehicle / mecha / starship facing
west; again, for the grid configuration for something facing east, just flip the grid configuration for the west-facing
configuration.
Hex Grid with Associated Flanks and Firing Arcs (West-East)
203
Hex Grid with Associated Flanks and Firing Arcs (Northwest-Southeast)
Like the other hex grids, the northwest-southeast grid is flipped along the vertical axis to give the
northeast-southwest grid, and it is flipped along the horizontal axis to give the southwest-northeast grid. When
flipped along both the vertical axis and the horizontal axis you have the southeast-northwest grid.
Starship Facings and Infrastructure
Every starship has 5 basic locations for damage; the 4 outer facings, known as the front (“fore”), the rear
(“aft”), the left side (“port'), and the right side (“starboard”), as well as an internal Hit Die total, known as the
“infrastructure” (IS). Every starship's Hit Dice (HD) are divided evenly between these 5 locations, with any
remainder assigned to the Infrastructure. Thus, every starship’s facings are designated as follows, based on the
polyhex it occupies; Fore (front), Forward Port (front left), Forward Starboard (front right), Aft (rear), Aft Port (rear
left), and Aft Starboard (rear right).
The hex an attack originates from will determine which side of the starship is hit by the attack. A forward-
204
facing weapon can fire on any hex within the arc ranging from the forward-port hex to the forward-starboard hex,
and any attack originating from any of those hexes can target the front of the starship. Similarly, a rear-facing
weapon can fire on any hex within the arc ranging from the aft-port hex to the aft-starboard hex, and any attack
originating from any of those hexes can target the aft of the starship. The arcs of the port and starboard sides are
identical, ranging from the forward to aft on their respective sides.
Damaging and Disabling a Starship
Most starship weapons deal damage in capital dice (D), increments of 20 HP. Only a full increment of 20
HP counts as a capital die of damage (1D). Put another way, a single attack must inflict 20 or more points of
damage to count as a capital die of damage; multiple lesser attacks that add up to 20 or more points of damage do
not constitute capital damage. Furthermore, most starships have stellar-scale armor offering 1D or 2D Hardness to
resist damage. Thus, in most cases, an attack must deal at least 40 points of damage, 2 capital dice of damage, to
damage a starship with 1D Hardness; 20 points / 1D to overcome the ship’s hull hardness, and 1D to inflict 1D of
damage to the ship. Similarly, an attack must deal at least 60 points of damage (3D) to inflict 1D of damage to a
starship with a Hardness of 2D.
In order to disable a ship, it's infrastructure must be reduced below 0D; this represents the destruction of
the ship's critical operating systems, rendering it effectively useless. Normally, a ship's infrastructure can only be
damaged if one of its sides has been breached, which is to say, when one of its sides has first been reduced to 0D.
This represents a hull breach that can now be exploited in destroying the ship's vitals. Once an outer facing of the
starship (aft, fore, port, or starboard) has been reduced to 0D, attacking ships can begin damaging the ship's
infrastructure by targeting attacks on the destroyed facing. When a starship's infrastructure is reduced to 0D, it is
“disabled” (see “Disabled” below); once it is reduced to -(½ IS)D or less, begins “breaking apart” (see “Breaking
Apart” below).
However, a starship's infrastructure can be damaged before reducing one of its outer facings to 0D;
whenever an attacking ship scores a critical hit on a starship, it assigns ½ of the inflicted damage to the
infrastructure and ½ the damage to the outer facing upon which the critical hit was scored. Also, attacking the ship
from within, either through sabotage or boarding party, inflicts damage directly to the starship’s IS. This represents
an attack that has breached the hull of the ship and damaged the ship's interior, usually causing casualties and/or
systems damage.

When a starship’s Infrastructure (IS) is reduced to 0 HP/d/D, it becomes Disabled. The ship can only take a
single move or attack action each turn (not both); it cannot jump to cruising speed or take any other full-round
actions. If it attacks, attempts to escape at cruising speed, or performs any other action that would strain its
systems, it takes 1 point of damage proportionate to its HP/d/D after completing the act.

If a ship’s Infrastructure (IS) is reduced to -50% of its original total, it begins breaking apart. No
longer capable of being repaired, the ship is a total wreck, only good for salvage. If the ship had maintained any
operational capabilities up until this point, they begin collapsing into a nonfunctional state; no sensors, no
propulsion, no weaponry, no shields, no life support. It takes a Gargantuan or smaller ship in space 1d2 rounds to
break apart, while Colossal ships 1d4+(1 per additional category of Colossal size) rounds to finish completely
breaking apart.
T/ACtical Armor Class
In E&E, a character’s Armor Class (AC) is represented as T/AC, which is their touch AC (T) compared to
their total AC (AC). This gives the range of attack results that hit the character’s armor versus hitting the character
directly. Touch AC is the minimum result required to make contact with the character, while total AC is the
minimum result required to make contact with an unarmored part of the character and the minimum result
required to confirm a critical hit against the character.
T/AC = Touch AC / Total AC
For example, a 1st-level Strong Hero (+1 Defense Bonus) with a 12 Dex (+1 Dex modifier) who has the
Heavy Armor Proficiency feat opts to wear full plate armor (+8 equipment modifier to AC, Hardness 10, HP 40).
205
This character’s touch AC is base 10 + Defense Bonus (+1 in this case) + Dex modifier (+1), touch AC 12. Adding the
+8 equipment modifier from the character’s full plate, we calculate the Strong Hero’s total AC at 20. Thus, this
armored hero’s T/AC is 12/20.
Touch AC = 10 + Defense Bonus (DB) + Dex modifier + other possible modifiers
Total AC = Touch AC + Equipment (Armor and/or Shield) bonus + Natural AC + possible others
What does that mean? It means that any attack result of 11 or less misses, a result of 12 to 19 hits the
character’s full plate, and a result of 20 or better hits the character directly. When the attack hits the armor, it still
deals damage as normal, but now the damage is reduced by the armor’s Hardness (in this case, 10 points), and the
remainder is applied to either the armor’s HP or to the wearer’s HP. Where the damage is applied is decided by
the wearer if they are proficient in the worn armor or determined by the attacker if the wearer is not proficient.
Now consider the 1st-level Fast Hero (+3 DB) with an 18 Dex (+4 modifier) who has Light Armor Proficiency
wearing a suit of leather armor (+2 equipment modifier, Hardness 2, HP 10). Let’s say this Fast Hero has also taken
the Dodge feat (+1 dodge modifier to AC, meaning it applies to both touch AC and total AC). This character’s T/AC
is 18/20, meaning to-hit results of 17 or less miss completely, 18-19 hits the character’s leather armor (Hardness 2)
with the remainder of the damage being applied to either the character or their armor (proficient character’s
choice), and a result of 20 or higher does its damage to the Fast Hero directly.
This Fast Hero gets hit 30% less often than the Strong Hero given above (Touch AC 18 versus Touch AC
12). However, when the Fast Hero is hit it is usually direct damage (with a range of only 2 results to hit the armor
18-19), and even if it does hit the armor it offers little protection (2 Hardness, 10 HP). Put another way, the Strong
Hero gets hit 30% more often than the Fast Hero, but in those instances the blow is hitting the full plate (10
Hardness, 40 HP), damaging the Strong Hero significantly less, if at all.
As seen here, touch Armor Class is easier to hit than total Armor Class, as it ignores natural modifiers from
thick skin, scales, or the like, as well as ignoring equipment modifiers to AC like armor and shields. This means that
successful hits occur more often using the T/ACtical ruleset. However, this increase in hitting is offset by the fact
that the armor absorbs (some of) the damage, plus characters can possibly parry and/or dodge in E&E combat.

A natural AC bonus gives a character a natural Hardness rating of 1 per +1 of Natural AC, and a
bonus 5 hit points. This natural hardness is applied to any physical damage (except acid damage) or any naturally-
occurring energy damage (except sonic damage) suffered. Disintegration, negative energy (as well as positive
energy), and null energy attacks ignore hardness, including natural hardness.
Unlike artificial hardness from armor or shields, which only apply if the armor or shield is hit, natural
hardness applies against every attack that hits the character. Natural hardness and artificial hardness stack, such
that an attack that hits a character’s armor must inflict enough damage to overcome the armor’s hardness, and
then any remaining damage has to overcome the character’s natural hardness to actually inflict any damage to the
character. If something ignores hardness, like a magical weapon or an armor-piercing bullet, it also ignores natural
hardness.
However, natural armor does NOT stack with artificial armor for purposes of being hit. Instead, a
character’s natural armor class modifier is only added to the total AC of the character for purposes of confirming a
critical. In the case of a character with artificial and natural armor modifiers, they will effectively have a “T/A/C”,
giving their touch AC, their total AC which includes their armor and shield modifiers for determining when the
character is hit versus when their armor/shield is hit, and finally their critical confirmation AC, which is their total
AC plus their natural armor modifier.
For example, a lizardfolk (natural AC modifier of +5) is wearing a breastplate (equipment AC of +5) with
Medium Armor Proficiency. Assuming the character has a Dex of 10 and no Defense bonus modifiers, the
character would have a T/A/C of 10/15/20; a touch AC of 10, a total AC of 15 with their breastplate, and a critical
confirmation armor class of 20, meaning critical threat rolls require a result of 20 or higher to confirm a critical
against the character. If the character is hit by a to-hit roll of 10-14, then the breastplate is hit, and the hardness of
the breastplate is applied initially, then the character assigns the remainder of the damage to the armor and/or the
character, although they will likely want to assign at least 5 points of the damage to the character, because their
natural hardness will absorb it. On a to-hit roll of 15 or higher, the lizardfolk character is hit directly; they apply
206
their natural hardness only to the damage, with the remainder going against the character’s HP. Finally, if the
character is hit with a critical threat (a natural 20, for example), then the attacker needs to get a result of 20 or
higher on the confirmation roll to confirm the critical.
Armor & Shields: Proficient characters get to assign where damage is taken whenever their armor is hit by physical
damage (i.e., acid, ballistic, bludgeoning, force, piercing, and slashing damage). Energy sources of damage (i.e.,
cold, electricity, fire, sonic, concussion, and untyped energy) are typically treated like physical damage, assigned
according to the armor-wearer’s / shield-bearer’s proficiency. If the energy source is an area effect that allows a
Reflex save, then a successful save is resolved like a physical attack, with the armor-wearer / shield-bearer
assigning the damage according to their proficiency.
However, a failed save against the area attack means full damage is taken by the wearer, and now the
wearer must make a saving throw for each item on their person, including their armor and/or shield, Fort DC 15 (+
1 for every 5 HP of damage beyond the item’s hardness in potential damage suffered, if preferred). Note that
enchanted items get a bonus to their save equal to their total enchantment modifier (i.e., +1 to +10 for non-epic
items); mastercrafted items get a modifier equal to their mastercrafted modifier (i.e., +1 to +3). Each item that
fails its Fort save also suffers full damage from the area effect, otherwise a successful save means it takes no
damage (shielded from the effect by the wearer’s body!).
In the case of a proficient character using an armor and/or shield who fails their save, they can assign up
to half of the damage from the area effect to the proficient armor and/or shield; apply the hardness as usual. In
many instances, players will elect to assign damage equal to their armor’s / shield’s hardness to the item without
surpassing the hardness, ensuring the item takes no damage itself, and they take the rest upon the wearer.
However, the wearer must always take at least half of the damage upon themselves on a failed Reflex save.
If an armor or shield reaches 0 HP, then it is broken. While broken it offers half the HP and armor class
modifier (rounded down), possessing no special enchantment or tech abilities if continuing to be used for defense,
purely serving as an intervening object. If the broken object is reduced to 0 HP or less again while broken, then it is
destroyed; it falls to pieces, shattered and useless. Note that something that is broken can be repaired, whereas
something that is destroyed cannot.

The T/ACtical ruleset also allows for the proper incorporation of power armor rules. Power armor is
the apex of personal armor and mecha, offering the best of both worlds. It operates like body armor in most ways,
but it is technically defined as “a mecha the same size category as its pilot”. Thus, a Medium creature wearing
power armor is in effect a pilot piloting a Medium-sized mecha.
However, just as mecha can be destroyed, power armor can be damaged and destroyed too. Unless
otherwise noted, all TS 6 and higher power armors are assumed to have the Environmental Seal gadget, and thus
all attacks, regardless of whether they hit the total AC, apply the armor’s Hardness to reducing their damage, as
the wearer is covered head-to-toe in the armor. In this sense the total AC for a proficient power armor wearer is
only needed for purposes of confirming criticals, otherwise every attack that beats the touch AC hits the armor.
Like normal armor in the T/ACtical combat system, the proficient character must decide how much
damage the armor takes and how much the character takes whenever damage does get through the Hardness of
the power armor.
Also, a critical threat, when it is first scored, must be deemed by the power-armor proficient character as
either a critical threat against their armor (which uses the Mecha Critical Hit chart), or a critical threat against the
character (then resolved as normal, but all damage is inflicted to the character, with only the armor’s hardness
being applied).
If the character wearing the power armor is non-proficient, then the attacker gets to choose where the
threat is resolved. Also, if the attacker has the feat Improved Sunder, then they can declare that they are attacking
the armor, regardless of the wearer’s wishes. Just remember, the critical threat still requires a confirmation roll
against the character’s total AC, incorporating the power armor’s equipment AC modifier.
If the character is using a shield, its AC modifier also increases the total AC required for confirming any
critical hits. If the character has a natural armor bonus, then its armor class bonus applies to the confirmation roll
required to score a critical only if the defender opts to have the potential critical strike them directly; if the
character chooses to have the threatening attack be resolved against their power armor, then their natural armor
207
bonus does not apply to the total AC required to confirm the critical.
If a power armor is reduced to 0 HP then it is broken, and it offers no further access to any tech built into
the armor. It is the equivalent of a basic body armor of the same type (light, medium, or heavy), with half the
equipment AC modifier and half the HP of the original power armor.
A key difference between a power armor pilot and a mecha pilot is that a power armor pilot gets to apply
their Defense Bonus to their touch AC (mecha pilots apply their Defense Bonus only to their total AC).
Conversely, a power armor wearer can still be targeted by spells that require line of sight to the target; for
example, Charm effects or Instant Death effects typically require line of sight to the target. Thus, such effects
could target a power armor pilot, but they could not target a mecha pilot (i.e., one where the mecha is one or
more size categories larger than the pilot). In essence, the mecha puts a wall between the pilot and any who
would target them, while a power armor is form-fitting and, like an armor, allows the wearer to be targeted.

As mentioned above, power armor is a special type of mecha, insofar that it is a mecha the
same size category as its pilot/wearer. Otherwise, a standard mecha is always one or more size categories larger
than its pilot. Depending on its size, it may have one or more co-pilots and/or gunners, with the largest
(Gargantuan+) mechas having room to carry troop units. Even larger than mecha are starships, massive vessels
built to traverse the stars.
Thus, Armor Class is determined a little differently for starships, as they are much larger, easier-to-hit
targets. A mecha’s / starship’s Touch AC is determined like a Medium-sized target, except they suffer size
modifiers the larger they are. Being so large, a proficient pilot does not apply their Defense Bonus to the mecha’s /
starship’s Touch AC, instead applying it to the total AC in helping protect the mecha / starship from critical hits. A
non-proficient pilot does not apply their Defense Bonus to any aspect of the mecha’s / starship’s AC.
Mecha & Starship Touch AC = 10 – Size modifier + Dex modifier + other modifiers (Ace Pilot’s DB?)
Mecha Total AC = Mecha Touch AC + Pilot’s Defense Bonus + Equipment AC Modifier of Mecha’s Armor
Starship Total AC = Starship Touch AC + Pilot’s Defense Bonus + (Hardness of Starship Armor / 5)
For example, a Large mecha made of Krithium (-1 Size modifier, base Dex 8, +10 equip AC modifier) with a
+4 Dex upgrade (Dex 12, +1 modifier) is piloted by a proficient 2nd-level Fast Hero (Dex 14, Defense Bonus +4). This
mecha’s T/AC is (touch AC is base 10 -1 for size +1 for Dex equals) 10/24 (Touch AC 10 +4 Defense Bonus +10
Krithium armor equipment AC modifier). The Fast Hero, despite having a Dex of 14 and therefore a +2 Dex
modifier, can only add +1 to the mecha’s AC because the mecha’s Dex is 12, and the pilot always uses the worse
Dex modifier (time for another Dex upgrade maybe!).
As mentioned above, mecha basically behave like mobile armored (typically self-contained) rooms where
the pilot sits, meaning that mecha and starship pilots cannot be targeted by any spells, powers, or abilities from
that require line of sight from outside their vehicle. Damage is always done to the vehicle and only the vehicle,
unless a critical result mentions crew casualties.

As Tech constructs, mecha and power armor are susceptible to critical hits. To confirm a
critical against a mecha, the mecha’s full Armor Class, for purposes of confirming a critical, is equal to their touch
Armor class plus one-half the mecha’s Hardness (rounded up), plus the pilot’s Defense Bonus plus their Shield
equipment AC modifier, assuming the pilot is proficient in both the mecha and in the shield. Other modifiers might
include the pilot’s luck or insight bonuses to Armor Class.
Whenever you confirm a critical hit against a mecha, you may choose to roll a d20 and consult Table:
Mecha Critical Hits instead of dealing the normal critical hit damage for the attack. However, you must accept the
results of the roll, even if those results are less than desirable.
Find below a chart for determining to-hit locations on bipedal and quadrupedal mecha; roll a d20 to see
where the critical hit struck the mecha. As the body parts are smaller than the body as a whole, an attacking
creature suffers a penalty to hit when targeting a specific body part; see the column regarding the penalties to hit
certain parts of the mecha’s body.
There is no penalty to hit a mecha when specifically targeting its torso, but if the result of the roll to-hit
208
would miss after applying the special -4 targeting penalty given below, then the attack still hit the mecha, but it
struck another area of the mecha’s body instead; roll 1d4 on the table below to determine which arm or leg was
hit instead (or a d6 or d8, if more appropriate based on the design of the mecha being targeted).

Each crewmember aboard the mecha, including its operator, must succeed on a Fortitude save (DC
15) or be dazed for 1 round. Unable to act, a dazed character can take no actions, but still retains their full Defense
Bonus.

One piece of equipment (attacker’s choice) is damaged and ceases to function until
repaired. It can be a flight system, sensor system, defense system, weapon (integrated only), or miscellaneous
system. Repairing a damaged system requires 1 hour of work and a successful Repair check (DC 20).

One piece of equipment (attacker’s choice) is destroyed and ceases to function. It can be a
flight system, sensor system, defense system, weapon (handheld or integrated), or miscellaneous system. A
destroyed system cannot be repaired, only replaced.

The force of the attack knocks the mecha prone. All crewmembers and passengers aboard
209
take 1d6 points of bludgeoning damage as they are knocked about their cockpits. A prone mecha takes a –4
penalty on melee attack rolls and can’t use thrown ranged weapons. The mecha gains a +4 bonus to Defense
against ranged attacks, but it takes a –4 penalty to Defense against melee attacks. Standing up from prone is a
move action that provokes attacks of opportunity.

The attack bypasses the mecha’s structure. Apply normal damage to one crewmember or passenger
(determined randomly), ignoring the mecha’s hit points; only apply the mecha’s hardness.
Roll critical hit damage using a x5 multiplier instead of the weapon’s normal multiplier.

The mecha automatically drops what it is holding and can take no attack or move actions for 1
round. While the mecha is stunned, the operator is not stunned.

Built to withstand the rigors of far space, TS 6 and higher starships always deal in capital dice (D).
Starships intended for battle are usually more heavily armored, with Hardness of up to 40 / 2D. Thus, it would take
60 HP / 3D of damage to inflict 1D to a starship with Hardness 2D; 59 hit points of damage or less would do nothing
to such a heavily armored starship.
Unlike the T/ACtical mecha rules where hit location is optional, hit location is crucial for starships.
Dividing their total D into five (5) equal portions for the Aft (A), Fore (F), Port (P), and Starboard (S) sides of the
ship, with the fifth portion going to the infrastructure (IS) of the ship, starships have tactical considerations as to
which flanks they expose during battle. Starfighters are highly effective in exploiting the weak side of a capital
ship, able to harass the exposed flank with superior maneuverability while in tight. Once a starship is reduced to
zero (0D) IS, then it is disabled, losing power until restored to at least 1D IS.
However, the Infrastructure can only be damaged in one of 3 ways; once one of the flanks (Aft, Fore, Port,
Starboard) is reduced to 0D, then the IS can be damaged through the open flank; or whenever a critical hit is
scored on the starship, then the damage done is equally divided between the flank and the IS of the ship; or the
starship is dealt damage from within the hull, perhaps by a boarding party or internal sabotage, with 100% of the
damage going to the IS. Once the ship reaches -50% of its Infrastructure, it is destroyed, breaking apart and/or
exploding.
Only the smallest starships, like Gargantuan starfighters or Ultralight-Colossal fast freighters, can
completely dodge incoming attacks. Otherwise, it is very easy to hit starships of Light-Colossal size or larger, owing
to their great size, and their Armor Class is more about avoiding critical hits than avoiding hits completely. Unless
otherwise noted, crew are not damaged when their starship is damaged, nor can they take damage on the
starship’s behalf.

Whenever a starship has a critical hit scored against it, the resulting damage (after its
Hardness has been applied) is divided evenly between the flank upon which the attack was received (i.e., Fore,
Port, Starboard, or Aft) and the Infrastructure of the starship.
A critical hit with a starship weapon normally multiplies the weapon’s damage. Use the critical hit
resolution system whenever a critical hit is confirmed; the attacker rolls a d20 and consults Table: Starship Critical
Hit Results to determine the effects of the critical hit on the target.

A number of crewmembers and passengers are killed (this effect applies only if the ship isn’t
destroyed). Roll 1d10 to determine the number of crew fatalities and, if the ship carries passengers, 1d10 to
determine the number of passenger casualties. Only supporting GM characters are affected.
A starship with less than one-half of its normal crew complement takes a –2 penalty on all attack rolls and
checks. A starship with less than one-quarter of its normal crew complement takes a –4 penalty on all attack rolls
and checks. A starship with no crew flies on autopilot and cannot attack. If a crewless ship doesn’t have a
functional autopilot system, it is immobile. If this result is rolled again and the ship has no living crew or
passengers, ignore this aspect of the result.

On top of being a normal critical hit, a damaged system result means that the system in
question remains inoperable until it is repaired, which requires 10 hours of work and a successful Repair check (DC
30). A starship’s engineer (or engineering team) can perform jury-rig repairs on the system as a full-round action
with a successful Repair check (DC 25), but the repairs last only until the end of the battle (or until the system is
disabled again). During that round of jury-rigged repairs, the starship can continue to take actions.

One communications system of the attacker’s choice is disabled. If this result is rolled again and the
ship has no undamaged comm systems, ignore this result and reroll.

One defense system of the attacker’s choice is disabled. If this result is rolled again and the ship
has no undamaged defense systems, ignore this result and reroll.

The starship’s tactical speed decreases by 1,000 feet until the engines are repaired. If this result is rolled
again, the effect is cumulative. If the ship’s tactical speed has already been reduced to 0 feet due to engine
damage, ignore this result and reroll.

The starship is blinded until repaired. All the ship’s targets gain the equivalent of total concealment (50%
miss chance). If this result is rolled again, ignore the result and reroll.

The starship’s targeting system ceases to function. The starship loses the targeting system’s
equipment bonus on attack rolls until the system is repaired. Reroll if this result comes up again.

One of the starship’s beam weapons, projectile weapons, or missile launchers (attacker’s choice) ceases
to function. The weapon remains inoperable until it is repaired. If this result is rolled again and the ship has no
functional weapons, ignore this result and reroll.

On top of being a normal critical hit, one of the starship’s defensive systems
