Reputation Reputation is used to determine whether another non-player character (NPC) recognizes a player character (PC). Those who recognize the PC are more likely to help the PC or do what they ask, provided the reputation has a positive connotation to the NPC who recognizes the PC. A high Reputation bonus also makes it difficult for the PC to mask their identity. Most of the time, a PC doesn’t decide to use their reputation. The GM decides when a PC’s reputation can be relevant to a scene or encounter. At the moment it becomes relevant, the GM makes a Reputation check for an NPC who might be influenced in some fashion due to the PC’s fame or notoriety, as detailed below. Fame and Infamy Most characters with a high Reputation bonus (+4 or higher) are considered well known within their profession or social circle. Whether this has a positive or negative connotation depends on the point of view of the NPC who recognizes the PC. When an NPC has a positive opinion of a PC’s reputation, the PC is considered famous by that NPC. Fame, when recognized, provides a bonus to certain Charisma-based skill checks. When an NPC has a negative opinion of a PC’s reputation, the PC is considered infamous by that NPC. Also, at the GM’s option, a PC might be considered infamous in certain situations due to events that have transpired in the campaign. Infamy, when recognized, provides a penalty to certain Charisma-based skill checks. Using the Reputation Bonus Whenever the GM decides that a PC’s reputation can be a factor in an encounter, the GM makes a Reputation check (DC 25) for the NPC involved. A Reputation check is 1d20 + the PC’s Reputation bonus + the NPC’s Int modifer (Some Knowledge skill modifiers might apply instead of the Int modifier, if the PC would be well known in the field covered by the Knowledge skill.). Modifiers to the Reputation check depend on the PC and the NPC in question, as shown below. Note that if the NPC has no possible way of recognizing a PC, then the Reputation check automatically fails. If the NPC succeeds at the Reputation check, they recognize the PC. This provides a +4 bonus or a -4 penalty on checks involving the following skills for the duration of the encounter: Bluff, Diplomacy, Gather Information, Intimidate, and Perform. Situation Reputation Modifiers The PC is famous, known far and wide with either a positive or negative connotation +10 NPC is part of the PC’s professional or social circle +5 The PC has some small amount of fame or notoriety +2 44 The GM must decide that a PC’s fame or infamy can come into play in a given situation to make a Reputation check necessary. A character who doesn’t know, or know of, the PC can’t be influenced by their reputation. Wealth The Relationship Between Value & Wealth Part of the allure of the adventuring career is the prospect of “high-reward” in pursuing high-risk / high- reward ventures. As a character accumulates wealth, it will manifest in many forms; equipment, vehicles, real estate, investments, etc. Significant assets will want to be tracked by the character, especially relevant weapons and equipment for personal use. However, wealth can be subjective in value, especially in different scenarios and between different societies. In our own world, parts of it would be considered Tech Scale 6 (ie. the American military) while others would be Tech Scale 5. If a character from the Tech Scale 5 world wanted to acquire a Tech Scale 6 item (ie. a laser assault rifle), it would cost them extra. Conversely, an item that is normally Tech Scale 5 is that much cheaper in a Tech Scale 6 world, because it is older, obsolete technology. A watch using Tech Scale 3 technology that would have cost a sizeable amount in a Tech Scale 3 world is of negligible cost in a Tech Scale 6 world. The wealth system of E&E uses an abstract method of determining cost, depending on the Tech Scale of the item and the effective Tech Scale of the GM’s scenario and/or present circumstances. Every item has a Purchase DC, an initial “difficulty” to acquire, that is modified by scenario and circumstances; your GM will let you know of any such modifiers. Find below a chart of the Wealth scores / Purchase DC’s and their representative equivalent in the predominant currency (i.e., copper piece, dollar, or universal credit). Starting Wealth Score All characters begin with a base Wealth score of 20, plus any Starting Occupation modifier, +1 for having 1-4 ranks in a Profession skill, plus the Windfall feat modifier if taken, plus 2d4. While playing the game, players convert their Wealth score into the predominant currency value, using the chart above, to determine how much they have to spend. Purchasing Items and Purchase DC Modifiers Whenever your character wants to purchase something, look up the item’s Purchase DC, and ask the GM if there are any modifiers based on scenario and circumstances. Apply the GM’s modifiers, if any, to the Purchase DC of the item, and use the chart below to determine the item’s cost. In many cases, the Purchase DC will be as given in the book, but if you’re purchasing an item that is “Licensed” (+1 Purchase DC), “Restricted” (+2 Purchase DC), “Military” (+3 Purchase DC), or “Illegal” (+4 Purchase DC), you’ll need to account for those modifiers. Also, items from different Tech Scales than the market’s available Tech Scale will have modifiers (-2 Purchase DC for each Tech Scale of the item below the market’s, +5 Purchase DC for each Tech Scale of the item above the market’s). Note that higher Tech Scale items may be completely unavailable, and they are almost never more than one Tech Scale above the market’s Tech Scale. If a character wants something above the Tech Scale of the market, they’ll likely have to build it themselves. See the section on Equipment for further details. Similarly, in any scenario with arcane or divine magic, there will likely be influences from the Outer Planes exerted upon the party, especially as they grow in power and catch the attention of powerful beings. In similar fashion, just as the party is a very small organization of like-minded individuals, other groups with their own allegiances arise out of the background of the campaign, with their own agendas. Thus it is that Alignments and Allegiances almost inevitably become a part of every game scenario. 46 The nine Alignments represent the axes of Good vs. Evil and Law vs. Chaos in the moral capabilities of any sentient creature, with Neutral sitting at the fulcrum. Allegiances, conversely, are infinite in nature, insofar as they can represent any given group, organization, or ideology. Allegiances As allegiances cover more possibilities for specific allegiances, you should deal with those on a case-by- case basis with your GM. Generally, however, an allegiance gives a +2 bonus to Charisma-based checks involving others of the same allegiance. More specifically, a declared Allegiance is required to use the Oathbound feat. Allegiances have no minimum requirements when it comes to the GM’s Six Scales of the scenario. Alignments Alignments are required for Divine Scale 1 scenarios and Arcane scenarios where the Outer Planes are being used, as the forces of the gods compete for dominance. Find below a description of the nine alignments based on the Law/Chaos axis and Good/Evil axis. A creature’s general moral and personal attitudes are represented by its alignment: lawful good, neutral good, chaotic good, lawful neutral, neutral, chaotic neutral, lawful evil, neutral evil, or chaotic evil. Alignment is a tool for developing your character’s identity. It is not intended to be a straitjacket for restricting your character. Each alignment represents a broad range of personality types or personal philosophies, so two characters of the same alignment can still be quite different from each other. In addition, few people are completely consistent. How Alignments and Allegiances Impact the Game You will notice that Clerics, Monks, Paladins, and Saints, amongst others, have alignment restrictions. Conversely, you may come across characters with references to an allegiance. While alignments are always along the Law/Chaos axis and the Good/Evil axis, with Neutral in between, allegiances are more specific in nature, being an allegiance to a group usually. However, both have role-playing ramifications if they are not adhered to. In the case of Clerics, Saints, and the like, they can lose their special and spellcasting abilities if they violate their alignment. In other cases, a breach of allegiance may cause certain class abilities or feats to become unusable. Good versus Evil Good characters and creatures protect innocent life. Evil characters and creatures debase or destroy innocent life, whether for fun or profit. “Good” implies altruism, respect for life, and a concern for the dignity of sentient beings. Good characters make personal sacrifices to help others. “Evil” implies hurting, oppressing, and killing others. Some evil creatures simply have no compassion for others and kill without qualms if doing so is convenient. Others actively pursue evil, killing for sport or out of duty to some evil deity or master. People who are neutral with respect to good and evil have compunctions against killing the innocent but lack the commitment to make sacrifices to protect or help others. Neutral people are committed to others by personal relationships. Being good or evil can be a conscious choice. For most people, though, being good or evil is an attitude that one recognizes but does not choose. Being neutral on the good–evil axis usually represents a lack of commitment one way or the other, but for some it represents a positive commitment to a balanced view. While acknowledging that good and evil are objective states, not just opinions, these folk maintain that a balance between the two is the proper place for people, or at least for them. Animals and other creatures incapable of moral action are neutral rather than good or evil. Even deadly vipers and tigers that eat people are neutral because they lack the capacity for morally right or wrong behavior. Law versus Chaos Lawful characters tell the truth, keep their word, respect authority, honor tradition, and judge those who fall short of their duties. 47 Chaotic characters follow their consciences, resent being told what to do, favor new ideas over tradition, and do what they promise if they feel like it. “Law” implies honor, trustworthiness, obedience to authority, and reliability. On the downside, lawfulness can include close-mindedness, reactionary adherence to tradition, prejudice, and a lack of flexibility. Those who consciously promote lawfulness say that only lawful behavior creates a society in which people can depend on each other and make the right decisions in full confidence that others will act as they should. “Chaos” implies freedom, adaptability, and flexibility. On the downside, chaos can include recklessness, resentment toward legitimate authority, arbitrary actions, and irresponsibility. Those who promote chaotic behavior say that only unfettered personal freedom allows people to express themselves fully and lets society benefit from the potential that its individuals have within them. Someone who is neutral with respect to law and chaos has a normal respect for authority and feels neither a compulsion to obey nor a compulsion to rebel. They are honest but can be tempted into lying or deceiving others. Devotion to law or chaos may be a conscious choice, but more often it is a personality trait that is recognized rather than being chosen. Neutrality on the lawful–chaotic axis is usually simply a middle state, a state of not feeling compelled toward one side or the other. Some few such neutrals, however, espouse neutrality as superior to law or chaos, regarding each as an extreme with its own blind spots and drawbacks. Animals and other creatures incapable of moral action are neutral. Dogs may be obedient and cats free- spirited, but they do not have the moral capacity to be truly lawful or chaotic. The Nine Alignments Nine distinct alignments define all the possible combinations of the lawful–chaotic axis with the good–evil axis. Each alignment description below depicts a typical character of that alignment. Remember that individuals vary from this norm, and that a given character may act in accord with their alignment from day to day. Use these descriptions as guidelines, not as scripts. The first six alignments, lawful good through chaotic neutral, are the typical standard alignments for player characters. The three evil alignments are typically for monsters and villains. Lawful Good, “Crusader” A lawful good character acts as a good person is expected or required to act. They combine a commitment to oppose evil with the discipline to fight relentlessly. A lawful good character strives to always tell the truth, keep their word, help those in need, and speak out against injustice. They do so because of their belief that there is an ideal system in which all may thrive, but it is dependent on all within it abiding by its precepts. A lawful good character hates to see the guilty go unpunished, for it represents both an injustice to an injured party and a weakness or failure of the system. Lawful good is the best alignment you can be because it combines compassion and honor to create a sense of justice tempered with mercy. Neutral Good, “Benefactor” A neutral good character does the best that a good person can do. They tend to have a natural empathy for other sentient beings and are often devoted to helping others. For them, the Golden Rule (ie. “Do unto others as you would have them do unto you”) says it easy enough. Benefactors work with kings and governmental bodies but do not necessarily feel beholden to them. Neutral good is the best alignment you can be because it means doing what is good just for the sake of being good, allowing one to be flexible in doing what they feel is right. Chaotic Good, “Rebel” A chaotic good character acts as their conscience directs them with little regard for what others expect of them. They make their own way, working with a fundamental respect for others’ existence that makes them kind and accepting. They believe in goodness and right but have no use for laws and regulations, seeing them as little more than self-imposed mental constructs intended to restrict a being’s freedom. They bristle at the notion of 48 being robbed of their free will, such as when others try to intimidate them and tell them what to do. They follow their own moral compass, which, although good, may not agree with that of society. Chaotic good is the best alignment you can be because it combines a good heart with a free spirit to create a sense of moral rectitude undeterred by the laws or will of others. Lawful Neutral, “Judge” A lawful neutral character acts as law, tradition, or a personal code directs them. Order and organization are paramount to them. They may believe in personal order and live by a code or standard, or they may believe in order for all and favor a strong, organized government. For them, the absence of law is tantamount to a state of nature, little more than animals. Lawful neutral is the best alignment you can be because it means you are reliable and honorable without being a zealot. Neutral, “Undecided” A neutral character does what seems to be a good idea. They don’t feel strongly one way or the other when it comes to good vs. evil or law vs. chaos. Most neutral characters exhibit a lack of conviction or bias rather than a commitment to neutrality. Such a character thinks of good as better than evil—after all, they would rather have good neighbors and rulers than evil ones. Still, they’re not personally committed to upholding good in any abstract or universal way. Some neutral characters, on the other hand, commit themselves philosophically to neutrality. They see good, evil, law, and chaos as prejudices and dangerous extremes. They advocate the middle way of neutrality as the best, most balanced road in the long run. Neutral is the best alignment you can be because it means you act spontaneously as circumstances dictate, without prejudice or compulsion. Chaotic Neutral, “Free Spirit” A chaotic neutral character follows their whims. They are an individualist first and last. They value their own liberty but don’t strive to protect others’ freedom. They avoid authority, resent restrictions, and challenge traditions. A chaotic neutral character does not intentionally disrupt organizations as part of a campaign of anarchy. To do so, they would have to be motivated either by good (and a desire to liberate others) or evil (and a desire to make those different from himself suffer). A chaotic neutral character may be unpredictable, but their behavior is not totally random. They are not as likely to jump off a bridge as to cross it (but they probably wouldn’t be averse to jumping off the bridge if it meant avoiding the authorities!). Chaotic neutral is the best alignment you can be because it represents true freedom from both society’s restrictions and a do-gooder’s zeal; everything you do is according to your own agenda. Lawful Evil, “Dominator” A lawful evil villain methodically takes what they want within the limits of their code of conduct without regard for whom it hurts. They care about tradition, loyalty, and order but not about freedom, dignity, or life. They play by the rules but without mercy or compassion. They are comfortable in a hierarchy and would like to rule, but they are willing to serve. They are willing to condemn others not according to their actions but according to race, religion, homeland, or social rank. However, they are loathe to break laws or promises, as it undermines the very system which they hope to leverage for power. Some lawful evil villains have particular taboos, such as not killing in cold blood (but having underlings do it) or not letting children come to harm (if it can be helped). They imagine that these compunctions put them above unprincipled villains, but ultimately the ends justifies the means for the lawful evil villain. Some lawful evil people and creatures commit themselves to evil with a zeal like that of a crusader committed to good. Beyond being willing to hurt others for their own ends, they take pleasure in spreading evil as an end unto itself. They may also see doing evil as part of a duty to an evil deity or master. Lawful evil is sometimes called “diabolical,” because devils are the epitome of lawful evil. 49 Lawful evil is the most dangerous alignment because it represents methodical evil, capable of surviving within an orderly system, proving successful all-too-often. Neutral Evil, “Malefactor” A neutral evil villain does whatever they can get away with. They are out for themselves, pure and simple. Unlike the chaotic neutral character, who is constantly out to prove their freedom, the neutral evil character is constantly out to prove their power. They shed no tears for those they kill, whether for profit, sport, or convenience. They have no love of order and hold no illusion that following laws, traditions, or codes would make them any better or more noble. On the other hand, they don’t have the random nature or self-destructive love of conflict that a chaotic evil villain has. Some neutral evil villains hold up evil as an ideal, committing evil for its own sake. Most often, such villains are devoted to evil deities or secret societies. Neutral evil is the most dangerous alignment because it represents pure evil, unbounded by concepts like honor yet reliably ruthless. Chaotic Evil, “Destroyer” A chaotic evil character does whatever their greed, hatred, and lust for destruction drive them to do. They are hot-tempered, vicious, arbitrarily violent, and unpredictable. If they are simply out for whatever they can get, they are ruthless and brutal. If they are committed to the spread of evil and chaos, they are even worse. Thankfully, their plans are haphazard, and any group they join or form is poorly organized. Typically, chaotic evil people can be made to work together only by force, and their leader lasts only as long as that leader can thwart attempts to topple or assassinate them. Chaotic evil is sometimes called “demonic” because demons are the epitome of chaotic evil. Chaotic evil is the most dangerous alignment because it represents the perpetual threat of random death and destruction, a constant source of uncertain terror. Character Philosophies and Religions Every character is going to have some sort of philosophy or religion, some sort of position or perspective, that motivates them to adventure in the first place. Whether it’s vengeance or justice, a lust for power or the quest for knowledge, characters are going to be doing what they’re doing for a reason. Allegiances are pretty straightforward; the character has some sort of political agenda, insofar as they are “allied” to some organization. Alignments give a more fundamental direction to the character, motivated by a personal set of morals and ethics. For some, that set of morals and ethics stems from a religion, the worship of a more powerful being believed to be responsible for the character’s fate and being. For Clerics, Druids, Paladins, Rangers, and Saints, religion is the cornerstone of their being, drawing their power from their god. Depending on your GM’s scenario, if divine spellcasters are available (ie. the scenario is a minimum Divine Scale 1 scenario), then there are gods to contend with in your world (!). There are many pantheons of gods available from our own mythology; from the Greeks and Romans to the Norse or Egyptian or Indian cultures, to name just a few, your GM has a wide array of gods with which to furnish their multiverse. However, the concepts those gods encompass are universal in nature; they represent fundamental aspects of being. From life and healing to war and death, from magic and mind to nature and knowledge, the gods have their spheres of power, and are revered because of their supremacy in their sphere. Given below are some prototypical godly roles, and their typical domains of power. Before Your Character Became a Hero Regardless of the existence of the gods, your character will have had a life prior to your playing them. Using the character’s Starting Occupation, Alignment, and Allegiances (if any), you should be able to put together some sort of background for your character. Even if you don’t determine anything else for your character, these fundamental aspects should be enough to give the GM and other players an idea of what your character is about. Of course, if you have any ideas for a particular backstory (sometimes called “fluff”) for your character, you should consider writing something to chronicle it. By giving your character a backstory, you bring the character to life, something that feels like it always existed, before you brought it to life, and you’re just stepping in now when the true heroics of the character’s story are needed. The more you tease it out, the more your character will feel like its own being, both for you and for the other players (and GMs sometimes reward it!). A word of caution, though; you should always vet the GM with any potential backstory, just to ensure it works with the scenario at hand. For example, you may want to play the rich dilettante with a penchant for adventure, but the GM’s scenario is based on the characters being in a tough financial position as the impetus for accepting the mission they have in mind. If your character is starting out rich, then the party may have no need to bite on the GM’s adventure hook, causing the GM’s efforts in preparing the scenario to be wasted. Be a good sport and understand that your backstory is meant to complement the main storyline, not dominate it (unless that’s something both you and the GM have worked out). The Difference Between Hero, Basic, and Advanced Classes The Hero classes are recommended for their ease of use and straightforward progression. Even better, they have enhanced access to Action Points (AP’s), which are very useful for making your character look heroic (or maybe not look foolish) at the right moment. And consider further; If your GM is creating a Heroic Scale 5 or higher scenario, then you’ll want to know that only Heroes, characters with one or more levels in a Hero class, can spend their Action Points as Fate Points at crucial moments in the game. Similarly, if your GM is creating a Mutation Scale 5 or higher “super-powered” scenario, then the Hero classes are ideal for generating “super- heroes”. Thus, for several reasons, players should seriously consider taking a Hero class to start when they’re available. Unless your GM is creating a Heroic Scale 0 scenario, more commonly known as a “victims” or a “grimdark” setting wherein characters are expected to die, you should have access to the Hero classes. The only prerequisite for a Hero class is a minimum 13 in the associated attribute. However, Hero class levels are either taken at 1st level, or by GM’s permission. If a character qualifies for and wants to take more than 1 Hero class, then they can do so, taking 1st level in any Hero classes that they qualify for at 1st level, effectively starting as a multi-classed character (more on multi-classing later). 52 Basic classes are called such because they are available with the birth of civilization (ie. Tech Scale 1). Thus, they are available for more scenarios, with minimal character prerequisites. Such classes are forward- compatible, meaning they still have relevance for higher Tech Scale scenarios. Advanced classes are more specific in their specialty, and as such have more stringent feat and/or skill requirements. For your part as a player, it’s enough to know that every Advanced class requires a minimum 3rd level character to qualify for, owing to the character prerequisites. As soon as your character takes a level in an Advanced Class, they are now a multi-classed character. It is the necessary aspect of multi-classing that makes them Advanced Classes. Prestige classes are like Advanced classes in that they have prerequisites, but they usually involve a minimum Arcane, Divine, Mutation, Psionic, or Tech Scale, and they always require the approval of the GM (thus their “prestigious” nature). For that reason, Prestige classes are described further in the E&E GM’s Guide. Multiclassing Multiclassing in E&E is straightforward; if your character qualifies for the class, then they can take levels in it. If you have a character with two attributes higher than 13, then you can start your character as a 2nd-level character, with 1st level in each of the two Hero classes associated with those attributes. If your character has three attributes 13 or higher, then your character has the option of starting at character level 3rd, with 1st level in each of the three Hero classes associated with those attributes, or a 2nd level character with 1st level in any two of those 3 Hero classes, or a 1st level character in one of the Hero classes for which the character qualifies. The character receives all the modifiers for 1st level in each Hero class taken, including Base Attack modifiers, Defense Bonus modifier, save modifiers, Reputation modifiers, a 1st-level Talent for each Hero class, and the skill points for each Hero class. In the case of multiple classes starting at 1st level, the player selects which of their starting classes is considered 1st level for purposes of skill points (see more on that in the Skills section). Keep in mind that many classes start with a Base Attack modifier of +0, meaning that too much multi- classing can compromise one’s Base Attack modifier at later levels. However, it can also result in higher-than- average saving throw bonuses, as your character’s diversity of experience has exposed them to a wider array of effects. It all depends on whether you want a warrior-type focus who is going to want the highest Base Attack modifier possible, or you’re looking to play a certain type of “jack-of-all-trades” with a diverse combination of classes. Just remember that, despite the names of the classes as given in this book, unless a character goes around saying “hi, I’m a fighter/rogue”, it’s more likely that their actions will be interpreted by those around them and they will be given some sort of moniker. A savvy character can introduce themselves as a “bounty hunter” or a “hirebrand”, and that’s what they’ll be known as. The class names are intended to be generic and give an idea as to the class’ specialty, but they can be re-skinned as the GM and/or the player(s) require. See “Advancing Levels” below for more on multiclassing. Experience Points Experience points (XP) are the measure of what your character has learned, and it is through XP that your character unlocks new plateaus of power aka gains levels. A character earns XP by defeating opponents and completing objectives. GM’s may also award bonus XP for exceptional role-playing or significant plot progression. Experience points are typically earned at the end of a session, although situations where the characters are caught in medias res at the end of the session will usually have XP rewards deferred until the completion of the situation at hand. Once a character earns enough XP, they advance a level. Advancing a Level Each time a character attains a new level, they either increase one of their current class levels by one or they pick up a new class for which they qualify at 1st level. When a character increases one of their class levels by one, the character gets all the standard benefits that characters receive for attaining the new level in that class: more hit points, possible increases, Defense, and saving throws (depending on the class and the new level), a new class feature (as defined by the class), and new skill points. Skill points are spent according to the class that the character just advanced in. Skills are purchased at the cost appropriate for that class, remembering that skills from a character’s Starting Occupation are always considered class skills. In general, a character can have levels in as many different classes as there are classes. The only restriction is a character who has levels in any non-Hero class can no longer take levels in any new Hero classes (the Career Path rule); the character can only take levels in Hero classes they already have levels in. If a character has two or more classes that use different power point pools (ie. arcane, divine, psionic, and/or super power points), they must keep track of the different power point pools. If a character has two or more classes that use the same power point type, then they add those amounts together for one pool of that power point type. However, caster or manifester levels do not stack between Basic classes; only Prestige classes that add effective caster or manifester levels to another class stack with a Basic class for purposes of spell/power access and caster/manifester level. The bonus to caster/manifester level by the Prestige class only applies to the selected Basic class, chosen at the time of advancing a level in the Prestige class that gives the +1 caster/manifester level modifier. The Hero Classes The Hero classes are only available in a Heroic Scale 1 or higher scenario (ie. most scenarios). The Hero classes have two prerequisites; they require a minimum attribute score of 13 or higher in their related attribute, and they must be taken at 1st-level character (or with GM’s approval after that). They embody the six main attributes of the game, and each has access to unique Talents based on their Hero attribute. What Makes a Hero a Hero in E&E? 54 In E&E, the main difference between a Hero and any other type of character is their access to Action Points. Action Points give a player greater agency in determining their Hero’s fate, mitigating how the dice might negatively impact their character. Depending on the Heroic Scale of the scenario, a Hero’s Action Points may be capable of allowing them to achieve the truly impossible! Action Points Action Points provide characters with the means to affect game play in significant ways; as such, Action Points (AP) are only available in Heroic Scale 1 and higher scenarios. A character always has a limited amount of Action Points, and while the character replenishes this supply with every new level they attain, the character must use them wisely. Note that the AP pool replenishes at each level, and any unused AP are lost; AP cannot be accumulated from level to level. A character can always spend 1 AP to do one of these things: - Alter a single d20 roll, such as an attack, a skill check, an ability check, or a saving throw; - Use a class talent or class feature during your turn for which the expenditure of 1 AP is required. When a character spends 1 AP to improve a d20 roll, roll 1d6 and add the result to the d20 roll to help meet or exceed the target DC number. A character can declare the use of 1 AP to alter a d20 roll after the roll is made but only before the GM reveals the result of that roll (whether the attack or check or saving throw succeeded or failed). A character can’t use an AP on a skill check or ability check when they are taking 10 or taking 20. When a character spends 1 AP to use a class feature, they gain the benefit of the feature but don’t roll a d6. In this case, the AP is not a bonus to a d20 roll. Depending on the scenario’s Heroic Scale, a character may only be able to spend 1 AP a round. In such instances, if a character spends a point to use a class feature, they can’t spend another one in the same round to improve a die roll, and vice versa. Depending on the character’s level (see the table below), they may be able to roll more than one d6 when spending 1 AP. If the character does so, they apply the highest d6 result and disregard the other rolls. Character Level Action Point Dice Rolled 1st-7th 1d6 8th-14th 2d6 15th-20th 3d6 In Heroic Scale 2 and higher scenarios, Heroic Action Points are available to give the heroic character more options in performing death-defying stunts and surviving harrowing odds. In Heroic Scale 5 and higher scenarios, Action Points can be spent (permanently!) as Fate Points when the stakes are truly desperate. Heroic Action Points If your GM is offering a Heroic Scale 2 or higher scenario, then you’ll have access to Heroic Action Points for your Hero characters. There are 4 additional uses for Action Points when Heroic Action Points are allowed; - Heroic Effort (“Focus!”); a Hero character gets the full d6 (i.e., +6) bonus on the die for spending an AP when taking a full-round action instead of a standard or move action that uses a Heroic attribute; - Heroic Dodge (“Jump for your life!”); a Hero character can spend an AP as an immediate action to get a Dodge attempt against an attack roll that would otherwise reduce them to zero (0) hit points or less; - Heroic Resurgence (“Just catching my breath!”); a Hero character can spend an AP as a full-round action to recover 25% of their hit points (rounded up), up to a maximum of 50% of their total hit points; - Heroic Destiny (“Beat the odds!”); a character can spend an AP prior to making a d20 roll to give themselves a 2nd d20 for the roll, taking the better result for the check. Only characters with one or more levels in a Hero class can spend their Action Points as Heroic Action Points. 55 Fate Points A Fate Point (FP) is the permanent expenditure of an Action Point. There is one universal use for an FP available to all Hero characters, “Twist of Fate”, and then there are some additional uses of FPs for specific Hero character classes, depending on their chosen Talents; - Twist of Fate; the universal use of a Fate Point, a character can spend an FP to force a re-roll of any d20 result that directly affects the character, including enemy’s d20 rolls; - Maximum Effort; a Strong Hero with Extreme Effort can spend an FP as a move-equivalent action to Take 20 on a Str-based check, including a melee attack roll (an automatic hit threatening a critical); - Nick of Time; a Fast Hero with Defensive Roll can spend an FP as an immediate action to automatically succeed on a Defensive Roll attempt (take 50% damage from an attack that would kill or disable the hero); - No Time to Bleed; a Tough Hero with Second Wind can spend an FP as an immediate action to use Second Wind, recovering 25% of their total hit points, up to a maximum of 50% of their total hit points; - Eureka!; a Smart Hero with Linguist can spend an FP as a full-round action to Take 20 on an Int-based check, even if such a check normally takes more than a full round (such as Investigate and Research); - The Right Touch; a Dedicated Hero with Healing Knack can spend an FP as a standard action to heal another character 25% of their total hit points, up to a maximum of 50% of their total hit points; - Good and Lucky; a Charismatic Hero with Allegiance to Good can spend an FP as an immediate action in response to a failed saving throw to instead Take 20 on the saving throw, automatically succeeding. The Hero’s Gift Beyond their Action Points, every Hero is possessed of “the Hero’s Gift”, some ability above and beyond their peers that has always set them apart. This gift is an innate talent or feat that the character is known for. All characters who take their 1st level in a Hero class get to select either one additional Talent, or one additional feat from that Hero’s bonus feat list for which they qualify, known as the Hero’s Gift. For example, a first level human Strong Hero would have the starting two feats all characters receive, plus one feat for being human, with the possibility of another feat depending on what Starting Occupation the Strong Hero takes. The starting Strong Hero also receives a Strong Talent at 1st-level, plus the Hero’s Gift, the player’s choice of either another Strong Talent or one feat from the Strong Hero bonus feat list. A character only ever receives a Hero’s Gift at first level, no matter how many Hero classes they might multiclass into afterwards. Furthermore, in Heroic Scale 5 or greater scenarios, keep in mind that only Heroes (characters with levels in one or more Hero classes) have the option of spending Action Points as Fate Points; a very valuable ability to have in determining your character’s fate when the dice are being especially fickle…! The Career Path While a character is still only taking levels in Hero classes, they are permitted to multiclass into other Hero classes, as they continue to develop their heroic nature. However, once a character has one or more levels in a non-Hero class, then they may no longer multiclass into other Hero classes; they can only continue to develop in Hero classes that they already have one or more levels in. The character has now selected their “career path”, and their heroic nature is established. Strong Hero: Focusing on physical strength, this character is typically the most dangerous one in melee, hitting often and hard. Be a Strong Hero if you want to be able to hit, damage, bend, or break whatever stands in your way. Fast Hero: Taking one or more levels in Fast Hero means this character is exceptionally agile, coordinated, and/or quick. Be a Fast Hero if you prefer stealth and finesse with shadowy movements and athletic displays. Tough Hero: A Tough Hero has a knack for taking a hit and staying up, possessing a greater fortitude and durability than most. Be a Tough Hero if you want to be able to withstand damage and be amongst the last standing when 56 the situation gets messy. Smart Hero: Usually the brains of the party, the Smart Hero is typically a bookworm, with an array of diverse knowledge and a tactical mindset. Be a Smart Hero if you want to be the character who can solve the situation when brute strength cannot prevail. Dedicated Hero: The Dedicated Hero is one with a wisdom beyond their years, guiding them on a path of moral principle that seems to offer them insight and willpower. Be a Dedicated Hero if you want a character who fights “the good fight”, or who has a connection with a greater power than themselves. Charismatic Hero: Whether through obvious physical comeliness or an unseen animal magnetism, the Charismatic Hero is typically the one at the center of the stage or action. Be a Charismatic Hero if you want to play a natural leader, or someone who has a glib tongue for swinging social interactions in their favour. If the hero has Favor, then they can also make a Suggestion to a Charmed target 1/day. If the hero has Captivate, then the Will save DC to resist being captivated is increased by +4. Fast-Talk Talent Tree The Charismatic Hero has an innate talent for bending the truth and dazzling others with a combination of words, mannerisms, and charm. Fast-Talk: The Charismatic Hero has a way with words when attempting to con and deceive. With this talent, they apply their Charismatic level as a competence bonus on any Bluff, Diplomacy, or Gamble checks the hero makes while attempting to lie, cheat, or otherwise bend the truth. Dazzle: Prerequisite: Fast-Talk. The Charismatic Hero has the ability to dazzle a target through sheer force of personality, a winning smile, and fast-talking. The target must have an Intelligence score of 3 or higher to be susceptible to a dazzle attempt, must be within 30 feet of the hero, and must be able to see, hear, and understand the hero. To Dazzle a target, the hero must use an attack action and make a Charisma check (DC 15), adding their Charismatic level (minimum +1) as a bonus. If the Charisma check succeeds, the target can try to resist. The target resists the Dazzle attempt by making a Will saving throw (DC 10 + Charismatic Hero’s class level [minimum +1] + Charismatic Hero’s Cha bonus). If the save fails, the target receives a -1 penalty on attack rolls, ability checks, skill checks, and saving throws for a number of rounds equal to the character’s Charismatic level (minimum 1 round). This talent can be selected multiple times, each time worsening the Dazzled penalty by -1. This is a Mind- Affecting ability. Taunt: Prerequisites: Fast-Talk, Dazzle. The Charismatic Hero has the ability to temporarily rattle and enrage a target through the use of insults and goading. The target must have an Intelligence score of 3 or higher to be susceptible to a Taunt, must be within 30 feet of the hero, and must be able to hear and understand the hero. To Taunt a target, the hero must use a standard action and make a Charisma check (DC 15), adding their Charismatic level (minimum +1) as a bonus. If the Charisma check succeeds, the target can try to resist. The target resists the Taunt by making a Will saving throw (DC 10 + Charismatic Hero’s class level [minimum +1] + Charismatic Hero’s Cha bonus). If the save fails, the target becomes fixated on directing their next action against the hero for the next round. This is a Mind-Affecting ability. Silver Tongue (Super-Talent): Prerequisites: Fast-Talk, Supernatural Mutation, 3 MP. The Charismatic Hero with a Silver Tongue receives their Fast-Talk modifier to all Bluff, Diplomacy, Gamble, Gather Information, and Intimidate checks. Also, the Silver Tongue can spend an Action Point to re-roll a skill check from the above-listed skills, but the character must accept the result of the second roll, even if it’s worse than the first roll. If the Silver Tongue can Dazzle, then the Dazzled penalty becomes equal to the hero’s Charisma modifier. If the Silver Tongue can Taunt, then they can attempt to Taunt a target as a move action if they wish. Leadership Talent Tree The Charismatic Hero has a talent for leadership and inspiration. 71 Coordinate: The Charismatic Hero has a knack for getting people to work together. When the hero can spend a full round directing their allies and makes a Charisma check (DC 10), the hero provides any of their allies within 30 feet a +1 bonus on their attack rolls and skill checks. The bonus lasts for a number of rounds equal to the hero’s Charisma modifier. The hero can coordinate a number of allies equal to one-half their Charismatic level, rounded down (to a minimum of one ally). Inspiration: Prerequisite: Coordinate. The Charismatic Hero can inspire their allies, bolstering them and improving their chances of success. An ally must listen to and observe the Charismatic Hero for a full round for the inspiration to take hold, and the hero must make a Charisma check (DC 10). The effect lasts for a number of rounds equal to the hero’s Charisma modifier. An inspired ally gains a +2 morale bonus on saving throws, attack rolls, and damage rolls. A Charismatic Hero can’t inspire themselves. The hero can inspire a number of allies equal to one-half their Charismatic level, rounded down (to a minimum of one ally). Greater Inspiration: Prerequisites: Coordinate, Inspiration. The Charismatic Hero can inspire their allies to even greater heights, bolstering them and improving their chances of success. An ally must listen to and observe the Charismatic Hero for a full round for the greater inspiration to take hold, and the hero must make a Charisma check (DC 10). The effect lasts for a number of rounds equal to the hero’s Charisma modifier. An inspired ally gains an additional +1 morale bonus on saving throws, attack rolls, and damage rolls, which stacks with the bonus from Inspiration for a total of a +3 morale bonus. A Charismatic Hero can’t inspire themselves. The hero can inspire a number of allies equal to one-half their Charismatic level, rounded down (to a minimum of one ally). Inspiring Aura (Super-Talent): Prerequisites: Coordinate, Supernatural Mutation, 3 MP. The Charismatic Hero with Inspiring Aura has a bolstering presence that always gives allies within 30’ a +1 bonus to their attack rolls and skill checks. When the character uses their ability to Coordinate, they can Coordinate a number of allies equal to their Charisma modifier (minimum 1 ally), giving an additional +1 bonus to attack rolls and skill checks that stacks with this one. If the character has Inspiration, then the ability can be used as a standard action. If the character has Greater Inspiration, then the additional bonus applied is +2, for a net morale bonus of +4 to the ally’s saving throws, attack rolls, and damage rolls when using Greater Inspiration. Apex Charismatic Super-Talent Karmic Crusader: Prerequisites: Two of Animal Magnetism, Silver Tongue, and/or Inspiring Aura, Supernatural Mutation, 11 MP. The Charismatic Super-Hero, when required to roll a d20, rolls 2d20, taking the desired result. Bonus Feats: At 2nd, 4th, 6th, 8th, and 10th level, the Charismatic Hero gains a bonus feat. This feat must be selected from the following list, and the Charismatic Hero must meet any prerequisites. Agile Riposte, Creative, Deceitful, Deceptive, Dodge, Iron Will, Jack of All Trades, Leadership, Lightning Reflexes, Low Profile, Negotiator, Persuasive, Point-Blank Shot, Renown, Trustworthy, Unstable Mutation I-V, Windfall. The Basic Classes Basic classes are available from 1st level. Like the Hero classes, the Basic classes have minimal prerequisites; they are usable for medieval scenarios onward (ie. Tech Scales 1+), and with some re-skinning are perfectly fine for more modern and futuristic campaigns. Here is a brief description of each of the Basic classes. A Quick Synopsis of the Basic Classes Aristocrat: Typically wealthy and/or politically powerful, Aristocrats specialize in the subtle powers of influence 72 offered by the upper echelon of society. Charisma is an Aristocrat’s key attribute. Bard: Originating from the skalds and minstrels of old, Bards are typically outgoing, itinerant musicians or orators, picking up esoteric bits of knowledge along their travels. Charisma is a Bard’s key attribute. Berserker: Warriors fueled by rage in the heat of the moment, Berserkers are fearsome to behold, capable of giving and receiving heinous injuries in battle. Strength is a Berserker’s key attribute. Cleric: A priest imbued with divine power, the Cleric possesses the favor of the gods. A specialized Cleric of nature is known as a Druid, who strives to maintain the natural balance. Wisdom is a Cleric’s key attribute. Expert: As the name implies, the Expert is a skilled artisan of diverse nature, a catch-all title for the types who would focus on skills more so than magic, psionics, or combat capabilities. Intelligence is an Expert’s key attribute. Fighter: The Fighter is the student of warfare, continually on the quest to better themselves in the art of war. Whereas the Berserker thrives on passion, the Fighter strives for strategy. Strength is a Fighter’s key attribute. Monk: Seeking the paths of inward enlightenment, the Monk abandons the aesthetic aspects of the world, turning their attention inward to master their own mind and body. Constitution is a Monk’s key attribute. Paladin: Dedicated to the vanquishing of evil, the Paladin has a strength of will and purpose that few can match, let alone exceed. Their efforts do not go unrewarded by their gods. Wisdom is a Paladin’s key attribute. Psion: A potent psychic specialized in one of the six schools of mental mastery, the Psion is capable of great and terrible manifestations born purely of the mind. Intelligence is a Psion’s key attribute. Ranger: A guerrilla fighter emphasizing stealth and finesse, the Ranger has an innate connection to nature, and a special hatred for a Favored Enemy. Dexterity is a Ranger’s key attribute. Rogue: The Rogue is a scoundrel, a scout, and a sneak who strikes from the shadows. With their training in trapfinding, Rogues are considered near-indispensable for most expeditions. Dexterity is a Rogue’s key attribute. Saint: A divinely-ordained representative of their deity, a Saint wields the power of their god with an instinctive ease. They are zealous in their devotion, at one with their god-given purpose. Charisma is a Saint’s key attribute. Sorcerer: Seemingly possessed of an inborn arcane power, Sorcerers are feared, and rightly so; no two Sorcerers are the same, save their unpredictably dangerous nature. Charisma is a Sorcerer’s key attribute. Warmind: The Warmind divides their efforts in self-mastery between the mental and the physical worlds, learning powers and techniques that augment their combat capabilities. Wisdom is a Warmind’s key attribute. Wilder: Possessing potent psychic powers fueled by passion, the Wilder is aptly named. A frenzied flurry of psionic power on the battlefield, the Wilder eludes attacks with impossible ease. Charisma is a Wilder’s key attribute. Wizard: The Wizard is a formal student of the ritualized arcane arts. With spellbook in hand, the Wizard has an arsenal of magic solutions for almost every problem. Intelligence is a Wizard’s key attribute. How the GM’s Six Scales Affects Basic Class Availability Depending on the Six Scales of your scenario, one or more of these classes may be unavailable. The Berserker and the Fighter are always options. If there’s no magic in your GM’s world, then the Bard, Sorcerer, and Wizard are ruled out. If there are no psionics, then the Psion, Warmind, and Wilder would be unavailable. If there are no gods, then the Cleric, Paladin, Ranger, and Saint are unavailable. If there is no established society or technology, akin to living in the Stone Ages, then there are no Aristocrats, Clerics, Experts, Rogues, or Wizards. Aristocrat Whether born of high society or aspiring to join it, the Aristocrat harnesses the power of their society to do their bidding. It is through diplomacy and business (or deceit and bribery) that the Aristocrat gains prestige and power. Campaign Prerequisites: Minimum Tech Scale 1 scenario. Hit Die (of the Hero): d6 (1d3+3) Action Points: Aristocrats gain a number of Action Points equal to their Charisma modifier [minimum +0, maximum +5] + one-half their character level, rounded down, at 1st level and every time they attain a new level in this class. Class Skills: The Aristocrat’s class skills (and the key ability for each skill) are: Appraise (Int), Bluff (Cha), Diplomacy (Cha), Disguise (Cha), Forgery (Int), Gamble (Wis), Gather Information (Cha), Handle Animal (Cha), Intimidate (Cha), Knowledge (all skills, taken individually) (Int), Listen (Wis), Perform (Cha), Profession (Wis), Read/Write/Speak Language (none), Ride (Dex), Sense Motive (Wis), Spot (Wis), Swim (Str), and Survival (Wis). The Starting Occupation the character selects can provide additional class skills to choose from. Skill Points at 1st Level: (6 + Int modifier) x5. Skill Points at Each Additional Level: 6 + Int modifier. Starting Feats: In addition to the two feats all characters get at 1st level, an Aristocrat begins play with the Simple Weapons Proficiency feat, Martial Weapons Proficiency feat, Light Armour Proficiency feat, Medium Armour Proficiency feat, Heavy Armour Proficiency feat, and the Shield Proficiency feat. Influence: An Aristocrat knows how to leverage reputation into power. They use “favors” that they can dole out or they can call in, as circumstances warrant. This works like the Charismatic Hero’s Favor talent, except the Aristocrat uses their Reputation modifier for the Favor check. For every successful Favor called in, the Aristocrat suffers a -1 Influence modifier to their Reputation score, until they can “return the favor”. Your GM will help you determine how a favor can be returned, and thus remove the -1 Influence modifier. In a similar vein, an Aristocrat can grant Favors. The Aristocrat can make a Reputation check DC 20 to see if someone in aristocratic circles needs a Favor; confirm with your GM before rolling to see if there are any circumstance modifiers to be considered for the Reputation check when proactively looking to fulfill a Favor. Conversely, one such as a fellow Aristocrat or a Charismatic Hero may approach the Aristocrat for a Favor (a great lead-in for adventure hooks!). In either case, the GM will provide the specifics, and the Aristocrat can decide whether or not to try and fulfill the Favor. If the Aristocrat does fulfill the Favor, and the fulfillment of the Favor is public in nature, then the Aristocrat receives a +1 Influence modifier to their Reputation score going forward. Multiple public Favors provide bonuses that stack, but the maximum Influence modifier an Aristocrat can have to their Reputation score is equal to their Charisma modifier. Conversely, if the Favor is private in nature, then the Aristocrat simply has a Favor that they can automatically call in with that individual; no Favor check is required (unless the Favor requested is not commensurate with the Favor originally gained, GM’s adjudication), and the Favor does not give the Aristocrat a negative Influence modifier. Note than an Aristocrat can owe multiple Favors, generating a maximum negative Influence modifier up to their Reputation score. In such a case, the Aristocrat’s Reputation score is not actually 0; it simply represents the maximum amount of Influence that they wield. While an Aristocrat’s Influence modifier is the negative equivalent of the character’s Reputation score, making it effectively zero (0), they cannot “call in” any more Favors. When a Favor is called in, the indebted Aristocrat must make an attempt to pay it back, or else suffer a permanent -1 modifier to their Reputation as an “oathbreaker”. They need not always pay back immediately, or in the way that the benefactor necessarily had in mind (this is where the Aristocrat’s social skills come into play!), but they must pay it back in some way that fulfills a mutually agreed-upon contract between the two parties. Decorum: Every budding Aristocrat has a natural bent for one of the social skills. Select one Charisma-based class skill and receive the Skill Focus feat for that skill. Improved Competence: At 2nd, 4th, 6th, 8th, 12th, 14th, 16th, and 18th levels, the Aristocrat’s competence in one of their class skills improves; the character receives a +1 competence bonus to one class skill of their choice. Each time the Aristocrat receives an instance of Improved Competence, they must select a different class skill. Refinement: At 3rd level, the Aristocrat has developed a niche for a particular sphere of knowledge. Select one Intelligence-based class skill and receive the Skill Focus feat for that skill. Bonus Feat: At 5th, 10th, 15th, and 20th level, the Aristocrat selects a bonus feat from the following list of feats, keeping in mind the character must have any prerequisites for the feat in order to select it: Alertness, Combat Martial Arts, Confident, Deceitful, Deceptive, Defensive Martial Arts, Educated, Investigator, 75 Meticulous, Mounted Combat, Negotiator, Persuasive, Skill Focus, Track, Urban Tracking, Weapon Finesse, Weapon Focus. Mental Acuity: At 5th, 10th, 15th, and 20th levels, the Aristocrat’s mind is better honed for their efforts; the character gains an innate +1 to one of their three mental attributes (+1 to Int, Wis, or Cha, player’s choice). Windfall: At 7th and 13th levels, the seasoned Aristocrat’s well-established business dealings have resulted in a bumper crop of yields; take the Windfall feat. Leadership: At 9th level, the veteran Aristocrat has built a business or political structure that includes a confidante / 2nd-in-command; receive the Leadership feat. Renown: By 11th level the Aristocrat’s adventures and exploits have become known, giving the character a certain amount of fame (or infamy!) that they can leverage; the character gains the Renown feat. Land & Title: The Aristocrat’s political maneuverings and/or legendary exploits have gained them favor with the highest power in the land, and they have been granted a piece of territory and formal title for their accomplishments. In game terms, the land is the equivalent of a +4 Wealth score bonus, while the title gives the Aristocrat an additional +1 bonus to Reputation and a Steward. The Steward is a second Cohort who represents the will of the Aristocrat in either foreign affairs or domestic affairs. In the case of a domestic affairs Steward, the Cohort must have at least 1 level of Bodyguard. In the case of a foreign affairs Steward, the Cohort must have at least 1 level of Ambassador. Otherwise the Steward is exactly like a Cohort, utterly loyal to the Aristocrat and their agenda. Bard The Bard comes in many forms; storyteller, thespian, musician, jester, demagogue, to name but a few. What all Bards have in common is a way with words capable of stirring the souls of those who hear them. In fact, a Bard’s mastery of words is so great it even gives them access to the arcane arts. Hit Die (of the Hero): d6 (d3+3) Action Points: Bards gain a number of Action Points equal to their Charisma modifier [minimum +0, maximum +5] + one-half their character level, rounded down, at 1st level and every time they attain a new level in this class. Class Skills: The Bard’s class skills (and the key ability for each skill) are: Appraise (Int), Balance (Dex), Bluff (Cha), Climb (Str), Concentration (Con), Craft (Int), Decipher Script (Int), Diplomacy (Cha), Disguise (Cha), Drive (Dex), Escape Artist (Dex), Gamble (Wis), Gather Information (Cha), Hide (Dex), Jump (Str), Knowledge (all skills, taken individually) (Int), Listen (Wis), Move Silently (Dex), Perform (Cha), Profession (Wis), Read/Write/Speak Language (none), Sense Motive (Wis), Sleight of Hand (Dex), Spellcraft (Int), Swim (Str), Tumble (Dex), and Use Magic Device (Cha). The Starting Occupation the character selects can provide additional class skills to choose from. Skill Points at 1st Level: (6 + Int modifier) x5. Skill Points at Each Additional Level: 6 + Int modifier. Starting Feats: In addition to the two feats all characters get at 1st level, a Bard begins play with Simple Weapons Proficiency feat, Light Armour Proficiency feat, Shield Proficiency feat, and the following specific Weapon Proficiency feats; longsword, rapier, sap, shortsword, shortbow, whip. Spells (Arcane Scale 1+ Scenarios): A Bard casts arcane spells, which are drawn from the Bard spell list. They can cast any spell they know without preparing it ahead of time. Every Bard spell has a verbal component (singing, reciting, or music). To learn or cast a spell, a Bard must have a Charisma score equal to at least 10 + the spell. The Difficulty Class for a saving throw against a Bard’s spell is 10 + the spell level + the Bard’s Charisma modifier. Like other spellcasters, a Bard can cast only a certain number of spells per day. Their base daily arcane power point allotment is given on Table: Bard Class Statistics by Level. In addition, they receive bonus power points per day if they have a Charisma score 12 or higher. Table: Bard Spells Known assumes the Bard has a sufficiently high Charisma (10 + the spell level to be able to learn and know spells of that spell level); a Bard requires a minimum Charisma of 16 to be able to know 6th-level Bard spells. The Bard’s selection of spells is extremely limited. A Bard begins play knowing four 0-level spells of your choice. At most new Bard levels, they gain one or more new spells, as indicated on Table: Bard Spells Known. (Unlike power points per day, the number of spells a Bard knows is not affected by their Charisma score; the numbers on Table: Bard Spells Known are fixed.) Upon reaching 5th level, and at every third Bard level after that (8th, 11th, and so on), a Bard can choose 77 to learn a new spell in place of one they already know. In effect, the Bard “loses” the old spell in exchange for the new one. The new spell’s level must be the same as that of the spell being exchanged, and it must be at least one level lower than the highest-level Bard spell the Bard can cast. A Bard may swap only a single spell at any given level, and they must choose whether or not to swap the spell at the same time that they gain new spells known for the level. As noted above, a Bard need not prepare their spells in advance. They can cast any spell they know at any time, assuming they have not yet used up all their arcane power points. Storyteller (Arcane Scale 0 Scenarios): The Bard has honed their craft regarding the use of colorful language and engrossing performances; gain a +1 competence bonus to one Cha-based class skill of choice. Multiple instances of Storyteller may be applied to the same skill; in this case the competence bonuses given by Storyteller stack with each other. Bardic Knowledge: A Bard may make a special Bardic Knowledge check with a bonus equal to their Bard level + their Intelligence modifier to see whether they know some relevant information about local notable people, legendary items, or noteworthy places. (If the Bard has 5+ ranks in Knowledge (history), they gain a +2 bonus on this check.) A successful Bardic Knowledge check will not reveal the powers of a magic item but may give a hint as to its general function. A Bard may not take 10 or take 20 on this check; this sort of knowledge is essentially random. DC Type of Knowledge 10 Common, known by at least a substantial minority drinking; common legends of the local population. 20 Uncommon but available, legends known by only a few people. 25 Obscure, known by few, hard to come by. 30 Extremely obscure, known by very few, forgotten by most who once knew it, known only by those who don’t understand the significance of the knowledge. Bardic Music: Once per day per Bard level, a Bard can use their song, poetics, or oratory to produce magical effects on those around them (usually including themselves, if desired). While these abilities fall under the category of Bardic Music and the descriptions discuss singing or playing instruments, they can all be activated by reciting poetry, chanting, making a speech, singing lyrical songs, singing melodies, whistling, playing an instrument, or playing an instrument in combination with some spoken performance. Each ability requires both a minimum Bard level and a minimum number of ranks in the Perform skill to qualify; if a Bard does not have the required number of ranks in at least one Perform skill, they do not gain the bardic music ability until they acquire the needed ranks. Starting a Bardic Music effect is a standard action. Some Bardic Music abilities require concentration, which means the Bard must take a standard action each round to maintain the ability. Even while using bardic music that doesn’t require concentration, a Bard cannot cast spells, activate magic items by spell completion (such as scrolls), or activate magic items by magic word (such as wands). Just like casting a spell with a verbal component, a deaf Bard has a 20% chance to fail when attempting to use Bardic Music. If they fail, the attempt still counts against their daily limit. Countersong (Su): A Bard with 3 or more ranks in a Perform skill can use their music, poetics, or oratory to counter magical effects that depend on sound (but not spells that simply have verbal components). Each round of the Countersong, they make a Perform check. Any creature within 30 feet of the Bard (including the Bard) that is affected by a sonic or language-dependent magical attack may use the Bard’s Perform check result in place of its saving throw if, after the saving throw is rolled, the Perform check result proves to be higher. If a creature within range of the Countersong is already under the effect of a noninstantaneous sonic or language-dependent magical attack, it gains another saving throw against the effect each round it hears the Countersong, but it must use the Bard’s Perform check result for the save. Countersong has no effect against effects that don’t allow saves. The Bard may keep up the Countersong for 10 rounds. Fascinate (Sp): A Bard with 3 or more ranks in a Perform skill can use their music, poetics, or oratory to cause one or more creatures to become fascinated with them. Each creature to be fascinated must be within 90 feet, able to see and hear the Bard, and able to pay attention to the Bard. The Bard must also be able to see the creature. The distraction of a nearby combat or other dangers prevents the ability from working. For every three levels a Bard attains beyond 1st, they can target one additional creature with a single use of this ability. To use the ability, a Bard makes a Perform check. Their check result is the DC for each affected creature’s 78 Will save against the effect. If a creature’s saving throw succeeds, the Bard cannot attempt to fascinate that creature again for 24 hours. If its saving throw fails, the creature sits quietly and listens to the song, taking no other actions, for as long as the Bard continues to play and concentrate (up to a maximum of 1 round per Bard level). While fascinated, a target takes a –4 penalty on skill checks made as reactions, such as Listen and Spot checks. Any potential threat requires the Bard to make another Perform check and allows the creature a new saving throw against a DC equal to the new Perform check result. Any obvious threat, such as someone drawing a weapon, casting a spell, or aiming a ranged weapon at the target, automatically breaks the effect. Fascinate is an enchantment (compulsion), mind-affecting ability. Inspire Courage (Su): A Bard with 5 or more ranks in a Perform skill can use song, poetics, or oratory to inspire courage in themselves and their allies, bolstering them against fear and improving their combat abilities. To be affected, an ally must be able to hear the Bard sing. The effect lasts for as long as the ally hears the Bard sing and for 5 rounds thereafter. An affected ally receives a +1 morale bonus on saving throws against charm and fear effects and a +1 morale bonus on attack and weapon damage rolls. At 8th level, and every six Bard levels thereafter, this bonus increases by 1 (+2 at 8th, +3 at 14th, etc.). Inspire Courage is a mind-affecting ability. Inspire Competence (Su): A Bard of 3rd level or higher with 7 or more ranks in a Perform skill can use their music, poetics, or oratory to help an ally succeed at a task. The ally must be within 30 feet and able to see and hear the Bard. The Bard must also be able to see the ally. The ally gets a +2 competence bonus on skill checks with a particular skill as long as they continue to hear the Bard’s music. Certain uses of this ability are infeasible. The effect lasts as long as the Bard concentrates, up to a maximum of 2 minutes. A Bard can’t inspire competence in themselves. Inspire Competence is a mind-affecting ability. Suggestion (Sp): A Bard of 6th level or higher with 10 or more ranks in a Perform skill can make a Suggestion (as the spell) to a creature that they have already fascinated (see above). Using this ability does not break the Bard’s concentration on the Fascinate effect, nor does it allow a second saving throw against the Fascinate effect. Making a Suggestion doesn’t count against a Bard’s daily limit on bardic music performances. A Will saving throw (DC 10 + 1/2 Bard’s level + Bard’s Cha modifier) negates the effect. This ability affects only a single creature (but see Mass Suggestion, below). Suggestion is an enchantment (compulsion), mind-affecting, language dependent ability. Inspire Greatness (Su): A Bard of 9th level or higher with 13 or more ranks in a Perform skill can use music, poetics, or oratory to inspire greatness in themselves or a single willing ally within 30 feet, granting them extra fighting capability. For every three levels a Bard attains beyond 9th, they can target one additional ally with a single use of this ability (two at 12th level, three at 15th, four at 18th). To inspire greatness, a Bard must perform and an ally must hear him perform. The effect lasts for as long as the ally hears the bard perform and for 5 rounds thereafter. A creature inspired with greatness gains 2 bonus Hit Dice (d10s), the commensurate number of temporary hit points (apply the target’s Constitution modifier, if any, to these bonus Hit Dice), a +2 competence bonus on attack rolls, and a +1 competence bonus on Fortitude saves. The bonus Hit Dice count as regular Hit Dice for determining the effect of spells that are Hit Dice dependent. Inspire Greatness is a mind-affecting ability. Song of Freedom (Sp): A Bard of 12th level or higher with 15+ ranks in a Perform skill can use music, poetics, or oratory to create an effect equivalent to the Break Enchantment spell (caster level equals the character’s Bard level). Using this ability requires 1 minute of uninterrupted concentration and music, and it functions on a single target within 30 feet. A Bard can’t use Song of Freedom on themselves. Inspire Heroics (Su): A Bard of 15th level or higher with 19 or more ranks in a Perform skill can use music, poetics, or oratory to inspire tremendous heroism in themselves or a single willing ally within 30 feet. For every three Bard levels the character attains beyond 15th, they can inspire heroics in one additional creature. To inspire heroics, a Bard must perform as a full-round action, and an ally must hear the bard perform. A creature so inspired gains a +4 morale bonus on saving throws and a +4 dodge bonus to AC. The effect lasts for as long as the ally hears the Bard sing and for up to 5 rounds thereafter. Inspire Heroics is a mind-affecting ability. Mass Suggestion (Sp): This ability functions like Suggestion, above, except that a Bard of 18th level or higher with 20 or more ranks in a Perform skill can make the Suggestion simultaneously to any number of creatures that they have already fascinated (see above). Mass Suggestion is an enchantment (compulsion), mind-affecting, language- dependent ability. Bonus Feat: At 5th, 11th, and 17th levels, the Bard receives a bonus feat. The feat may be any feat for which the Bard qualifies. 79 Magnum Opus: By 19th level the Bard has composed (at least) one epic ballad, a song that has begun to spread of its own accord across the land. The Bard gains the equivalent of the Renown feat, and they get a +2 circumstance modifier to all Cha-based skill checks when dealing with someone who recognizes them as the author of the ballad. Berserker Not so much a class as an inborn combat mentality, the Berserker is one who exults in the roar of battle. Once their blood reaches its boiling point, there is little save death that will stop a Berserker from attacking its quarry. Hit Die (of the Hero): d12 (d6+6) Action Points: Berserkers gain a number of Action Points equal to their Charisma modifier [minimum +0, maximum +5] + one-half their character level, rounded down, at 1st level and every time they attain a new level in this class. Class Skills: The Berserker’s class skills (and the key ability for each skill) are: Climb (Str), Craft (Int), Drive (Dex), Handle Animal (Cha), Intimidate (Cha), Jump (Str), Listen (Wis), Ride (Dex), Survival (Wis), and Swim (Str). The Starting Occupation the character selects can provide additional class skills to choose from. Skill Points at 1st Level: (4 + Int modifier) x5. Skill Points at Each Additional Level: 4 + Int modifier. Starting Feats: In addition to the two feats all characters get at 1st level, a Berserker begins play with Simple Weapons Proficiency feat, Martial Weapons Proficiency feat, Light Armour Proficiency feat, Medium Armour Proficiency feat, and Shield Proficiency feat. The penalty to AC remains at –2. Cleric A Cleric is a formal follower of a diety or principle, having been educated in esoteric tenets under holy tutelage. They learn powerful prayers to invoke the powers of their gods, and only if they are truly devout are their prayers answered. Campaign Prerequisites: Minimum Tech Scale 1 scenario for Cleric (does not apply to the Druid); minimum Divine Scale 1 scenario. Character Prerequisite: Alignment: A Cleric’s alignment must be within one step of their deity’s (that is, it may be 81 one step away on either the lawful–chaotic axis or the good–evil axis, but not both). A Cleric may not be true neutral unless their deity’s alignment is also true neutral. Hit Die (of the Hero): d8 (d4+4) Action Points: Clerics gain a number of Action Points equal to their Charisma modifier [minimum +0, maximum +5] + one-half their character level, rounded down, at 1st level and every time they attain a new level in this class. Class Skills: The Cleric’s class skills (and the key ability for each skill) are: Concentration (Con), Craft (Int), Diplomacy (Cha), Knowledge (arcana, history, religion, the planes, theology and philosophy) (Int), Profession (Wis), Spellcraft (Int), and Treat Injury (Wis). The Starting Occupation the character selects can provide additional class skills to choose from. Domains and Class Skills: A Cleric who chooses the Animal or Plant domain adds Knowledge (nature) (Int) to the Cleric class skills listed above. A Cleric who chooses the Knowledge domain adds all Knowledge (Int) skills to the list. A Cleric who chooses the Travel domain adds Survival (Wis) to the list. A Cleric who chooses the Trickery domain adds Bluff (Cha), Disguise (Cha), and Hide (Dex) to the list. See Domains, under Spells & Powers for more information. Skill Points at 1st Level: (2 + Int modifier) x5. Skill Points at Each Additional Level: 2 + Int modifier. Starting Feats: In addition to the two feats all characters get at 1st level, a Cleric begins play with Simple Weapons Proficiency feat, Light Armour Proficiency feat, Medium Armour Proficiency feat, Heavy Armour Proficiency feat, and Shield Proficiency feat. A Cleric who chooses the War domain receives the Weapon Focus feat related to their deity’s weapon as a bonus feat. They also receive the appropriate Martial Weapon Proficiency feat as a bonus feat, if the weapon falls into that category.
